en: A Direct Explanation of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (The Smaller Amitābha Sūtra):
Right Practice Compiled with Annotations by the Śramaṇa Liaogen of Juehai Monastery in Xiushui,
a Successor in the Dharma Lineage (Dazhi and Dachun), and Revised by Lay Disciples Daben, Ling, Daqing, and Chen.
△ Preface: Clarifying the Meaning of the Title.
The original title of this sutra is the *Sūtra on Immeasurable Equal and Pure Enlightenment*. It is also known as the *Sūtra on the Buddha of Infinite Life*.
The various masters who successively translated and revised the titles of this sutra are too numerous to list in full. Since the Tang dynasty, this sutra has been transmitted...
Upon arriving in China, Dharma Master Xuanzang translated [this work] as the *Sūtra on the Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddha’s Acceptance*.

The Master was a native of the Chen family from Luozhou; he left home to become a monk in his childhood and was immediately skilled in expounding upon the sūtras and the vinaya, earning him the title of a "divine man" at that time.
At the age of twenty-one, from the third year of the Zhenguan era, he traveled to the Western Regions to seek scriptures.
Having endured numerous hardships and traversed one hundred and fifty kingdoms, he eventually reached Śrāvastī, where he obtained more than six hundred fascicles of sutras;
this present *Miaofa Lianhua Jing* (Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra) is also included among them. Upon returning to the capital in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, the Master translated [them] by hand.
These works amount to over a thousand fascicles in total. What is now called the *Amitābha Sūtra* is the title translated by Master Kumārajīva.

Because the core teaching of this sūtra—the method of single-mindedly holding the Name—is what the masses most delight to hear, he established the title using these six characters so that all might believe, accept, and propagate it. The opening word "Buddha" refers to Śākyamuni Buddha.
He was the son of King Śuddhodana. The Buddha’s mother, Queen Māyā, gave birth to him on the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty.
His childhood name was Siddhārtha; at the age of twenty-five, he left the household life.

He went to Mount Gajaśīrṣa to practice meditative concentration. He allowed reeds to pierce his knees and permitted sparrows to nest upon his head. For six years he practiced such austerities, subsisting on nothing but hemp and wheat.
It was only when he beheld the morning star at night that he attained great enlightenment. Thereafter, he preached the Dharma to deliver sentient beings for forty-nine years.
He lived to the age of eighty before entering parinirvāṇa. More than one thousand years after his nirvāṇa, [it reached...]
In the eleventh year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, the teaching flowed into Zhendan (China). From that time until the present, more than one thousand years have passed.
Regarding the meaning of the word "Buddha" (*buddha*), it is said to mean "awakened. As for the words *Amitābha*, *a* means "non-" and *mitābha* means "measure";
therefore, he is also titled the Buddha of Immeasurable Life (*Amitāyus*). Someone asked: "What is this Amitābha Buddha?"

Question: Is he a person of the present age? Answer: All Buddhas possess the three bodies—the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body—and manifest according to the capacities of sentient beings.
If we speak in terms of specific events, even though they are transformational sages, such events must necessarily occur at a particular time.

However, this Amitābha Buddha has been preaching the Dharma throughout the past immeasurable kalpas, the future immeasurable kalpas, and the entirety of the present; thus, he may be briefly cited as being of the present.
To speak of it: immeasurable kalpas ago, there was a king in that region named Dharmākara.
He renounced his throne to leave the household life and made forty-eight vows to extensively deliver sentient beings; he is none other than the present Amitābha Buddha.
This is the Buddha accomplished by the bhikṣu Dharmākara, and yet Amitābha Buddha manifests himself at all times in response to the needs of beings.
In this world, for the sake of deluded and confused multitudes, he has practiced pure deeds and personally attained the state of Amitābha Buddha;
such instances are beyond counting. Therefore, in both preceding and succeeding dynasties, there have been those who manifested as Amitābha Buddha appearing in the world.
One who examines this meaning—how can it be definitively fixed? Furthermore, it was asked: "Since Amitābha is already..."
If one asks, "The Buddha of this kalpa is Śākyamuni Buddha, whereas Amitābha Buddha is currently preaching the Dharma;

are they not perhaps contemporaneous? The answer is: In the past, there was the Bodhisattva Jñānabodhi, who stated that the *Dhāraṇī-sūtra* speaks of thirty-seven Buddhas, all of whom are emanations of the single Buddha Vairocana from immeasurable kalpas ago. This Vairocana...
The Buddha-way possesses five wisdoms. First is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), which is its nature. Second is the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*), which is its essence.
Third is the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), which is its function. Fourth is the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), which is its faith.
Fifth is the Pure Wisdom (*viśuddha-jñāna*); this is the function within functions of Vairocana Buddha. It naturally occupies the center of the Dharma-realm.
Pure Wisdom. Next, from the four wisdoms, the Tathāgatas of the four directions flow forth.
Furthermore, the Wondrous Observational Wisdom flows forth to the Western World of Ultimate Bliss as Amitāyus Tathāgata; thus, one Buddha manifests simultaneously in two lands.
It can be known that Amitābha existed immeasurable kalpas prior to Śākyamuni Buddha, let alone this [present].
In the sutra, my Buddha has provided the evidence that since Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood, ten kalpas have passed until now.

Again, it was asked: "If this is indeed so, and this *Amitābha Sūtra* was spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha with his own mouth, for what reason does it also say that Amitābha Buddha currently manifests in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss?"

When asked about the Buddha’s ear of hearing the Dharma, he replied: "Our Buddha knows that Amitābha Buddha preaches the Dharma immeasurably according to the capacities of beings, vows to deliver immeasurable sentient beings, welcomes them with immeasurable light, and causes them to be born by transformation upon lotus flowers in immeasurable numbers."

If people of the present day single-mindedly uphold even a single phrase of the name of Amitābha Buddha with firm resolve and without regression, they will certainly be reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss at the time of death.

Although the Buddhas do not appear simultaneously, it can be said that Amitābha Buddha is still present. Therefore, one should not [limit this] by means of the three periods of past, present, and future.

This is merely an inference regarding transcendence. Yet, although the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas employ a thousand ways of preaching the Dharma and ten thousand methods of transformation and deliverance, for what reason do we ourselves not all become Buddhas?
Why is this? It is because both Buddhas and ordinary beings are, in essence, one and the same spiritual nature (*xingling*).
It is only that the Buddhas, through the power of their vows to uproot suffering, manifest in response to the world and enter among the various classes of beings to deliver them.
Although a person’s feet never cease their movement, the Buddha-nature within them is ever-illuminating and ever-awake; it is ever-awake and ever-illuminating.
It remains unchanged through the movement and stillness of past and present—this is what is called "Immeasurable Life. We ordinary beings are by nature fundamentally identical to this awakening.
However, because our minds cling to the heaviness of form and appearance, we are obscured by worldly desires and constantly turn our backs on that awakening. Though [our heads...]
Emerging from the depths and submerging back, one has long remained within the bright sun of a clear sky, yet it is as if one passes the days in the dead of night.
If one clarifies the meaning of this sutra, one will know that one's own mind has turned from darkness to light, like recovering a lost object;

is this not the greatest fortune of a lifetime? If people read this sutra or listen to its lectures, they must be careful not to let their minds wander or treat it with negligence. This is called [the Name].
It is said: "Receive and uphold this sutra. Although the matter is difficult to believe, nevertheless, strive to examine it closely once more.

When Huìróng went abroad on a journey, he met the King of Kucha, who gave him his younger sister in marriage. From her, he fathered Huìshī. When Huìshī was seven years old, he accompanied his mother to a monastery where he took a bowl upon his head;
at that moment, he suddenly awakened to the principle that "all phenomena are but mind. He immediately attained mastery of the doctrines and meanings of the Tripiṭaka.
The King presented a golden lion throne as an offering. At that time, the Grand Astrologer of the Qin state reported: "An extraordinary star has appeared in the western city.

Since such stars appear when great virtuous sages emerge, the King said: 'I know there is a Master Shi in Kucha who is profoundly attuned to the Buddha-dharma and capable of serving as a patriarch for future students;
could this not be him? He then dispatched a general to welcome the Master back to the kingdom."
The Master knew that the ruler of the state at the midway point, named Yao Chang, intended to harm him; thus, he took his leave and did not go to see him.

Later, Yao Chang also heard of the Master’s reputation and earnestly invited him, but the invitation was not granted. Upon Yao Chang’s death, his son Yao Xing again requested his presence, and only then did he comply with the invitation to join Yao’s court, thereby returning to Qin.
He served as the National Preceptor of Qin. Because he had been invited to return to Qin by the Yao father and son, it is so stated.

This was during the Yao Qin dynasty. The scriptures translated by the Master total more than three hundred sections. He elucidated their profound subtleties during the eleventh year of the Hongshi era.

At his death, his tongue remained undecayed; it is said that because the scriptures translated by the Master were the words of the Buddha and not false, his tongue manifested such a miraculous sign as a verification.

The Prince’s name was [Śuddhodana]. Furthermore, the monastic residence was called Jetavana, which is comparable to the Aranya, the Flower Palace, or the Deer Park.
The ruler of that country was titled King Prasenajit. The Buddha was the Teacher of the Kingdom of India;

having traveled to the neighboring kingdom of Śrāvastī, he encountered an elder named Anāthapiṇḍada, who beheld the Buddha’s noble countenance and majestic deportment, and his patience in the Dharma was beyond compare.
Anāthapiṇḍika immediately purchased Prince Jeta’s grove and adorned it with precious jewels to welcome and make offerings to the Buddha.
The prince said, "While the grove belongs to you, the trees do not. He insisted on cutting down the trees. The elder reflected:
The flowering trees were lush and flourishing, fit to serve as offerings for the Buddha. The Prince said, "For every leaf taken from these trees, one gold coin shall be paid.
The elder wished to pay this price, but the Prince’s mind shifted and his intention changed; he requested that the Buddha preach the Dharma, saying, "It should not be thus.
The Prince said, "You relinquish the garden, and I relinquish the trees; let us both be donors together. Thus it was with the elder.

In the center, he immediately constructed sixty-four great monasteries; the central one was for the Buddha’s residence, while the remaining ones were bestowed upon the orphaned, the solitary, and the destitute.
Moved by the Prince’s gift of the trees, they collectively named the site the Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma (the Jeta Grove, Gift of Anāthapiṇḍada).
He was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

"Together with" (yǔ) means that the Buddha also accompanied the multitude. "Bhikṣu" refers to the disciples of the Buddha whose preceptual conduct is without transgression and whose virtue and morality flourish together;
thus they are called bhikṣus. This is a general designation for eminent monks, similar to how one speaks of the six harmonies of the *saṃgha*.
The term *bhikṣu* carries three meanings: first, "mendicant" (*yācanaka*), for he begs for the Dharma to sustain his life of wisdom and begs for food to sustain his physical body;

second, "one who terrifies Māra," because he causes Māra to feel alarm and dread; third, "one who destroys evil," because he destroys the evils of the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
The title "Great" (*Bhadanta*) is an honorific designation for one of venerable virtue. When the Buddha was traveling, the bhikṣus attended upon him. One—
One day the Buddha instructed the bhikṣus, "Each of you go forth to wander and transform sentient beings;
I shall now go myself to the kingdom of Magadha. In that kingdom there are four Kāśyapas:
Mahākāśyapa, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, and Nadīkāśyapa. Each has two hundred and fifty disciples who maintain the sacrificial fire."
The non-Buddhist ascetic Nāga. When the Buddha traveled there late in the evening, he requested lodging from Mahākāśyapa.
Kāśyapa granted the Buddha’s request, providing him with a fire-dragon cave for rest. As the night grew deeper, the fire-dragon emitted flames from its seven apertures to burn the Tathāgata’s body.
The Tathāgata sat there, absorbed in the cool samādhi of Prajñā. These flames instead burned the dragon itself. When the dragon beheld the Tathāgata...

He placed a bowl of cool water before him and entered the mountain caves. Seeing the Buddha’s majestic radiance, Kāśyapa led his two hundred and fifty disciples to join the Buddha and renounce the householder’s life.
Subsequently, the other three Kāśyapas likewise led their respective disciples to follow the Buddha and ordain.
The Buddha then thought of King Bimbisāra and, leading the four Kāśyapas and their thousand disciples, entered Rājagṛha.
In the city, the king, knowing that the Buddha was coming, ordered his hundred officials to welcome the Buddha into the kingdom.

There was an elder named Kāla who saw the Buddha entering the country with the ruler and the people paying him reverent homage. As there was yet no vihāra, the elder immediately offered up the Bamboo Grove (Veṇuvana).
The king constructed palatial buildings, and invited the Buddha to dwell there in retreat. Later, the bhikṣu Aśvajit entered the village. Śāriputra...

I am still young and have studied the Way for but a short time; how could I understand the Tathāgata’s wondrous Dharma? He then spoke a verse, saying:
"The Buddha has taught all dharmas To eliminate all minds of men. When men have no minds at all, What [further] need is there?"
"Śāriputra, all dharmas must be heard. Upon hearing this verse, Śāriputra immediately awakened to the Tathāgata’s original intent.

He returned and informed Maudgalyāyana, who also attained awakening beneath those words. These two men together led two hundred and fifty disciples to leave the household life in reliance upon the Buddha.
Therefore, there were one thousand two hundred and fifty people in total.
All of them were great Arhats, well-known to the masses.
The phrase "all of them" refers back to the preceding text. "Arhat" is a Sanskrit term; in the language of Tang (Chinese), it means "one who is unattached.

This signifies being free from afflictions (*kleśa*), free from greed and hatred, and free from both opposition and compliance. Mind and objects are both empty, and inner and outer are eternally tranquil.

There is no dharma to be learned; this is called an Arhat. An Arhat can encompass four meanings: first, the Worthy One (*arhat*), who is a field of merit for humans and devas—the fruit of the mendicant (*bhikṣu*).
Second, the slayer of thieves, who has completely slain the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*)—the fruit of severing delusion.
Third, the one who stays far from evil, having utterly severed the three types of unwholesome thoughts; these three evils are greed, hatred, and delusion. [This is] the destruction...

This is the fruit of evil. Fourth is non-arising (*anutpāda*), which means not undergoing further existence; that is, when the delusions of the three realms are exhausted, one no longer undergoes birth.
This is the fruit of the terror of Māra. Even the learning of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is called true learning; therefore, it is termed "Great."
One who knows is not entangled by various marks, not bound by afflictions, not detained by thoughts and cravings, and not shrouded by ignorance;
therefore, this is called "knowing. As for "consciousness": where there is birth, there must be death;
where there is form, there must be decay. Thus, this stinking skin-sack, a mass of pus and blood—how could it be my permanent possession?
All that possesses marks is markless; it is not even the Way. To know the meaning of this ultimate principle is to have nothing to do;
therefore, it is called "awareness" (*vijñāna*). One should always allow the four great elements to be empty and the five aggregates to be non-existent, forgetting both person and phenomena.
This means there is nothing one does not know and nothing one does not recognize; this is called "knowledge of the wise.
If one can truly attain such power of mastery and maintenance in this way, they may be called a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
"Elder Śāriputra. The term "Elder" (sthavira) is an appellation for one whose years and virtue surpass others. It is not only Śāriputra who is called an Elder;
later, venerable ones such as Ānanda and others were all Elders. The Buddha was the foremost disciple among these.
My son, you are endowed with the three virtues of wisdom, vows, and practice, and are thus able to understand this sutra.
As for the two words "Elder" (sthavira) that the Buddha spoke first, they seem to serve as a general address. Śāriputra was mentioned at the outset because his wisdom is foremost;
Śāriputra is also named Śārigarbha (Son of the Śārī). His mother’s physical appearance was upright and graceful, and her eyes were like those of a śārika bird.
It is merely a title derived from his mother's name.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana means "Great Mung-bean" (*mahā-mudga*);
this is his clan name (*gotra*). As he was the eldest among a large number of kinsmen, he was thus named.
Mahākāśyapa, foremost in supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). *Mahā* means "Great.
*Kāśyapa* means "Tortoise-clan" (*kūrma-gotra*); in full, he is called "Great Tortoise-clan. His ancestor was moved by...

A numinous tortoise emerged carrying a divine diagram, and thus he was named after his clan. It is also said that he was called "Drinking Light" (Pītabhāsa) because in a previous life he had been a master metalworker;
when a poor woman offered him a gold bead for them to jointly repair a stupa and image, he subsequently attained a golden complexion in every lifetime and took this as his name.
He was able to maintain all forms of ascetic practice and was foremost among those who observe the dhūta precepts.
Mahākātyāyana— here translated as "Ornamented" (Wénshì)—

One who is well able to provide offerings to the sages and worthies of the four quarters, the zenith, the nadir, and the ten directions, and who practices the excellent fruits of the field of merit for humans and devas, is called the "First Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).
Kālodāyin— this is translated as "Black Light"—
so called because his physical form was coarse and his complexion black. Mahākapphiṇa.
This is called the lunar mansion *Hō* (Jyeshthā). His mother prayed to the star *Hō* and gave birth to him; thus, the mansion was used as his name.

Bakkula—here translated as "Good Appearance"—formerly practiced extensive giving and adorned himself with merit. He did not violate the precept against killing for ninety-one *kalpas*.

Four intermediate kalpas constitute one great kalpa (*mahākalpa*). Regarding "adornment" (*vyūha*), there are two meanings. First, the splendor of the Dharma-relics, such as incense, flowers, banners, and canopies—various kinds of offerings;

One should persevere in ascetic practices and cultivate the six pāramitās in equal measure. The six pāramitās are: giving, ethical discipline, diligence, patience, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

With every thought one remains unattached to the mundane world, and with every moment of mindfulness one returns entirely to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, ascending to be born by transformation among the nine grades of the Pure Land.
This constitutes internal adornment. As for not violating the precept against killing, [heavenly beings...]

To drown sentient beings—specifically by taking their lives—is precisely what is meant by shedding the blood of a Buddha.

As for those who eat their flesh, how could it not be the bodies of one's own parents? Thus, a sutra states: "Only those who murder their father, murder their mother, or murder an Arhat [commit this offense].
For this reason, the gentleman keeps his distance from the kitchen. Furthermore, fearing that cause and effect shall not fail, he ensures that life-for-life retribution is repaid.

Is this not a cause for awe? Having seen this Venerable One, who is thus adorned with compassion and mercy, and who will subsequently become a Buddha—his appearance so dignified and majestic, his lifespan reaching one hundred and sixty years, making him foremost in longevity.
Aniruddha means "Free from Poverty" (Wupin).
Because in a previous life during a time of famine, he once gave food to a Pratyekabuddha, his resources remained sufficient for eighty kalpas;
therefore, he was given this name. However, after he went forth as a monk, he constantly indulged in excessive sleep. The Buddha...

Regarding the phrase "these and other such great disciples," the Buddha did not exhaustively list them all for the sake of his followers. This follows upon the sixteen *sthaviras* mentioned above and serves as a concluding summary for the one thousand two hundred and fifty [monks] below.

It says, "The Sons.

Realization is called "awakening. Those who have not yet exhausted ignorance are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*). Because they can extinguish deluded thoughts by maintaining the single mind alone, a *mahāsattva* is here translated as "the mind of the Great Way";
this is the title for a Bodhisattva. Because they are first able to deliver others before being able to deliver themselves, an ancient worthy once said:
"One who encourages ten people to practice the recitation of the Buddha's name is called a 'good person. Up to...
Those who number in the hundreds or thousands are none other than Bodhisattvas practicing the stages of the Mahāyāna.
As for Mañjuśrī Dharma-rāja-putra—
Mañjuśrī is here translated as "Wondrous Head" (Miaoshou) and also as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode)— he is the foremost of the myriad practices and myriad virtues.
The Master extensively practiced skillful means to transform sentient beings through virtue; he was known as the Bodhisattva King Śrīkūṭa. As for the term "Dharma Prince":
the Buddha is the Dharma King, and when a Bodhisattva enters the stage of the correct position within the Dharma, they are called a Dharma Prince; they are also called a Son of the Buddha.
From the ancient sages and worthies down to this land, they have acted to perpetuate and flourish the seed of the Buddha, succeeding to the Buddha’s legacy.
Thus, Mañjuśrī has a vow to serve as the mother for the appearance of all Buddhas in the world;
our Buddha was the first to extol Mañjuśrī, designating him as the foremost among the Bodhisattvas in wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Ajita.
"Ajita" is Maitreya; he is also called Maitreya, which is his clan name, while "Ajita" is his personal name.
It is further said that Aśoka (Unconquerable) made a vow while in his mother’s womb: "May I, in my future life, attain the Samādhi of Compassionate Mind.
Whenever the kalpa of weapons occurs, may I protect and sustain sentient beings; if anyone is about to be harmed, I vow to take their place."
His great vow to rescue beings from suffering is unsurpassed. He occupies the rank of Lord of the Dragon Flower Assembly in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace;
it should be known that even the bodhisattvas in the celestial palaces arise from pure karma. As for what is called the realm of the dust motes and Ganges sands throughout the ten directions—
There is nowhere that is not a pure land. Therefore, in the past, the Venerable Vaidehī aspired to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
she sought the Buddha’s right concentration and fixed her mindfulness upon Amitābha Buddha.
The Bodhisattva Gandhahasti.

*Gandhahasti* means "Unresting" (*aviśrānta*). Because he is able to maintain the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and because the holy life consists of upholding the name of the Buddha so that the True Dharma (*saddharma*) circulates until its very extinction—his vow has no end, and thus he does not rest.
This is the mind of vastness alone.
As for the Bodhisattva Constant Diligence (*Sadāprarudita*):

Even if one were to live for immeasurable eons without attaining Buddhahood, one vows never to abandon them.
This great compassion, which constantly practices diligence, is called the ultimate offering of the True Dharma to the Tathāgata.

"Accompanied by such great bodhisattvas as these"—this phrase concludes the preceding section, implying the presence of Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and others, and should include Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, and all other bodhisattvas.
The Buddha is the foremost of those who have perfected the ten thousand practices of a bodhisattva; he protects and sustains sentient beings with mindfulness.
The Buddhas have equally realized the wisdom and vision of Amitābha; thus we may know that Bodhisattvas appear in the world to extensively deliver sentient beings one another.
As long as even a single sentient being has not attained Buddhahood, they remain seated at the site of enlightenment throughout the ten directions.
Since all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess such compassion to receive and guide sentient beings, how could we ordinary beings fail to practice the recollection of the Buddha?
"En. Anran fell into a state of despondency.

"Everyone" refers to those who all hear [the teaching] together. Śakra-devānām-indra is the lord among the gods;
that is, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. "Immeasurable" means including all the various devas throughout the thirty-three heavens.
"The great assembly" refers to everyone from the devas downward, including humans, asuras, and all sentient beings of the six realms. "Together" means that these...
The Bodhisattvas and the great assembly of devas were all present. To summarize what the Buddha said when he preached this sutra:

not only did the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, devas, humans, asuras, and all other sentient beings together ascend to the other shore, but even those below—including those in the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals—also realized the Samādhi of the Pure Land and suddenly shattered the profound darkness. Thus one may know the power of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation).
The Dharma rescues from suffering with great swiftness; thus, sentient beings of both good and evil are reborn in the Lotus Realm immediately.

Therefore, when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, devas and humans alike look up to it in reverence. Dragons and snakes mingle together; ordinary beings and sages intermingle. One must have faith that the Buddha-Dharma is maintained and sustained.
Simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
This sutra, from "Thus have I heard" up to "the great assembly of devas were all present," serves as the introductory section for attesting to its authenticity.
The Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the great assembly of devas gather from afar at one time; this is called the sixfold accomplishment.
Thus, "Thus" (*evam*) signifies the accomplishment of faith; "I have heard" (*śrutam*) signifies the accomplishment of hearing; "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) signifies the accomplishment of time.

The Buddha constitutes the accomplishment of the principal; a certain location constitutes the accomplishment of the place; and the assembly of listeners constitutes the accomplishment of the retinue.
All these emerge from the World-Honored One as the unique cause for exercising compassion to rescue and deliver sentient beings.

As for the meaning of the circulation of the orthodox teaching in the subsequent sections, it is as follows: for living beings of the present age who see or hear this sutra, they are as if in the direct presence of the Buddha.
I grant this personal prophecy so that you may be inspired to awaken the mind of enlightenment, draw near to Amitābha, and together escape the wheel of suffering. Do not harbor doubts or errors;
do not treat the Buddha with arrogance or turn your back on his grace.
△ Preaching the Dharma according to the capacity of the listeners.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Śāriputra:
"Whenever a Buddha preaches the Dharma, it is always because his disciples seek instruction in the discourse on non-duality; only then does he proclaim it."
It is the One Vehicle. Therefore, at the beginning of all other sutras, there is first a question posed, and then the World-Honored One initiates the teaching.

This *Amitābha Sūtra* alone is not taught because of such a request; rather, at that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Śāriputra, initiating the discourse himself as the starting point for his teaching. Why is this? Because the Buddha acts for the sake of sentient beings.

Those with dull faculties and deep karmic obstructions find it difficult to distance themselves from adverse conditions; unable to attain liberation through meditative concentration, they are submerged in birth and death with no prospect of escape.
Out of vast compassion, the Buddha pointed out the single gateway of the Pure Land, wishing that all sentient beings might transcend birth and death by traversing it horizontally.
It is like a person whose illness is critical and whose life hangs by a thread: when an excellent prescription is transmitted, one must practice according to the instructions.
If one were to prepare [a medicine] and delay the process, the medicine would not yet be finished when one’s life had already come to an end.
Yet, if there were medicine ready at hand, one would live as soon as it entered the mouth. The method of upholding the recitation of the Buddha's name is likewise so.

Because the Buddha wished to urgently rescue sentient beings from their afflictions, he preached this sutra without waiting for a request. However, the World-Honored One does not rely on written characters or spoken language.
This is the teaching of the Supreme Vehicle. Why, then, is this sutra further expounded? It is for the sake of those with superior faculties;

if they should open their mouths, it causes them to enter the gate of obstruction. As for those of middling and inferior faculties, they cannot avoid being enticed and led upward to reach realization.

Thus one may know, O World-Honored One, that establishing the Dharma spontaneously without waiting for prayer is an extraordinary act of compassionate grace, employing provisional means to deliver sentient beings.
This is the most urgent of all tasks. O benevolent ones, quickly administer the remedy; its benefit shall be inexhaustible.
If people are content with worldly pleasures, they do not realize that such pleasure is the cause of suffering. At the critical juncture of birth and death, one is utterly lost and without a shore.
Believe these words of the Buddha, uphold his name, awaken to your own nature, and suddenly emerge from the fiery pit. This is not possible unless you follow the Buddha.
How could one know the bliss of the Pure Land? Fortunately, having encountered the Buddha’s grace, he has specifically revealed a single method that yields immediate efficacy when practiced.
Those who wish to escape the wheel of suffering must act with urgency, not waiting for time to pass.
△ Marking the Land to Reveal its Basis.
"From here, to the west, beyond a hundred trillion Buddha-lands, there is a world named Sukhāvatī. Regarding "from here, to the west":
this indicates the direction of the West in response to our current location in this Sahā world. Regarding "beyond": it means from this land.
To go toward the west is called "passing through. A Buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*) refers to one great trichiliocosm;
reaching as far as ten trillion Buddha-fields means that, in terms of direction, it may indeed be called distant. However, according to phenomena it is distant, but according to principle it is near.
Regarding what is meant by "phenomena," the Sūtra says: there is a world named Sukhāvatī, which faces this Sahā [world].
To speak of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss as a Pure Land while it is a place of extreme suffering is to distance oneself from it most distantly.
According to principle, the self-nature is fundamentally pure; being free from hindrances and devoid of faults, it is this non-dual, tranquil mind.
Since this is the meaning of the natural, inherent nature, how could a mind that discriminates between far and near arise? Thus, even when one reaches [the ultimate],...
It is the Ultimate Bliss. Is this not close at hand? As the ancients said: "There is nowhere that is not the Pure Land.
That the Buddha specifically points to the West is to fix the mind's direction. Furthermore, when he speaks of a world named "Ultimate Bliss," what is this bliss?
It is the joy born of the mind; it is the bliss of attachment to objects—objects [that appear] in the world.
Cessation results in emptiness. One birth and one death follow as emotional conditions remain unsevered; thus, the holy path is difficult to accomplish.
Moreover, objects of perception may be either good or evil. Now, although the ultimate Way is good, even such objects cannot be maintained—how much less so evil objects?
If evil karma is deep, one will sink into the sea of suffering, revolving there without end. As for Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), it is a mind without objects. Without...
The mind is the root. When one severs the very source of hatred and attachment, this is precisely entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
There is no pleasure derived from any deliberate action; this is what is called "supramundane pleasure. Yet it is also not a pleasure at all.

This is what is meant by "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī). Because this bliss is inexhaustible, it is termed "ultimate. However, worldly people all prefer to calculate based on matters of immediate expediency. For example:
When selling goods, if one receives a price of one coin for two coins' worth, one will surely worry about it, considering it a loss of capital.
When traveling a long distance, if one covers the journey of a single day in two days, one will likewise surely worry, considering it a waste of time.
Thus, regarding minor losses of external things, even upon encountering such a loss, one still recognizes the cause for concern. Yet, why alone do you not worry about your own person? Its radiance—
The aggregates (skandhas) are finite. In a single day of impermanence, one becomes bewildered as to where one goes; this loss is exceedingly great.

How can one be so utterly lacking in discernment? Therefore, the Buddha emphasizes the gateway of mindfulness of the Buddha, wishing only that sentient beings may turn toward this inexhaustible bliss.
Exert yourself with single-minded diligence; you shall immediately ascend to that land and be named a Son of the Buddha. This benefit is no small matter—how could it not be a source of joy?
△ This marks the primary subject and reveals the correct teaching.
In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha, who is currently preaching the Dharma.
The word "that" (其) refers back to the preceding text; since a land must have inhabitants, it specifies the person who relies upon it by naming him "Buddha."

A Buddha must necessarily have a title; his title is Amitābha Buddha. When it is said that "the Buddha Amitābha is currently preaching the Dharma," this refers only to the fact that since Amitābha attained Buddhahood, ten kalpas have passed prior to the time of the World-Honored One [Śākyamuni]. How, then, can he be said to be "currently preaching the Dharma"?
This is because during the time the World-Honored One resided in the world, there were disciples who felt resentment toward their own meager merit and perceived obstacles.
"Alas! Though I have received the Buddha's teachings, I fear I shall not attain the Way.
If the World-Honored One were to enter parinirvāṇa now, I would no longer behold the Golden Tathāgata. Moved by such longing and lamentation, the Buddha comforted him, saying:
"As for the Amitābha Buddha in the West who currently preaches the Dharma, I do not say that there is a Buddha only after my own parinirvāṇa."
Furthermore, Amitābha Buddha constantly manifests emanations to preach the Dharma, delivering sentient beings throughout kalpas; how could this not be the present?
Because the faculties of the masses are shallow and they have not yet reached the ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*), they take refuge in forms and appearances.
Therefore, the Buddha commanded his disciples to focus exclusively on the Pure Land, showing them that they should choose what is good and follow it. This is the worldly...
The World-Honored One’s concern for the hearts of humanity is so urgent that he has made such an arrangement; this is truly an act of vast compassion.
If one examines this intent, it is clear that not only does Amitābha currently preach the Dharma, but the World-Honored One himself also continues to preach the Dharma even unto this day.

This is truly a profound aspiration spanning a thousand ages, intended to attract and guide people toward rebirth in the Pure Land, much like a boatman who entices travelers to board his vessel and delivers them to the other shore.
If people are willing to go, why not practice the daily recitation of the Buddha’s name?
First, you ought to investigate and break through this present life: its toil and suffering, its transient gathering of flesh and bone.
With a single stroke, sever this mind of emotional attachment forever; become a companion to the śrāvakas and attend the Buddha throughout the day. Why do people not exert themselves?
△ First, the general name "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī) is shown:

"Śāriputra, for what reason is that land called 'Ultimate Bliss'? Because the sentient beings in that country have no manifold sufferings and experience only various joys, it is therefore named 'Ultimate Bliss.'"

As for why that land is named "Ultimate Bliss" (*Sukhāvatī*): it is to recall the preceding passage and point out the name "Ultimate Bliss," thereby further causing sentient beings to give rise to a heart of great joy and inclination toward taking refuge in the Buddha-land.

Regarding the statement that "the sentient beings of that land have no manifold sufferings and experience only various joys": this refers to the two meanings of suffering and joy; citing their number makes them difficult to [fully] enumerate.

It is all exhausted. Thus, this person rushes about in the world, toiling and laboring; in old age, they are weary and decrepit; in sickness, they suffer pain and affliction; at death, they grieve over separation.

As for those they love, they desire union yet find only separation; as for those who are enemies, they desire to avoid them yet encounter them; as for what they seek, they desire to obtain it yet lose it.
Furthermore, they are oppressed and tormented by all manner of calamities and sufferings—this is the suffering within suffering. In that land, desire is abandoned.
Being pure, there is no suffering of suffering. Being born by transformation within lotus flowers, there is no suffering of birth.
Since cold and heat do not shift [the environment], there is no suffering of aging. Not receiving a womb-born body, there is no suffering of illness.

Manifesting as the Dharma-body, there is no suffering of death. That land also has no wives, children, or kinsmen; thus, there is no suffering of being separated from what is loved. Always following all...

Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not suffer from the pain of encountering those one hates. Furthermore, in this land, there is the constant suffering of not meeting a Buddha, whereas in that land, there is the joy of seeing a Buddha as soon as the flowers bloom.

In this land, there is the suffering of not having a Buddha personally preach the Dharma, whereas in that land, there is the joy of receiving a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) face-to-face from all Buddhas.
In this land, it is difficult to avoid the suffering of the three calamities and eight difficulties, whereas in that land, [it is] always...
In this land, there is the suffering of being entangled by treacherous and wicked companions;

in that land, there is the joy of dwelling together in harmony with all superior and virtuous people. In this land, there is the suffering of being constantly harassed and disturbed by hordes of demons;
in that land, there is the joy of being forever free from the evil realms. In this land, one is perpetually beset by impurities and worldly toil.
In this land, there is the suffering of the incessant cycle of saṃsāra; in that land, there is the bliss of the naturally sweet and harmonious sustenance of the life of wisdom.
In this land, there is the suffering of the brevity of lifespan; in that land, there is the bliss of longevity equal to that of the Buddha.
In this land, there is the suffering of hunger, cold, physical deformity, and pus and blood; in that land, there is the bliss of dhyāna.

There is the bliss of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). In this land, time passes swiftly and is spent in vain suffering; in that land, there is the bliss of attaining realization of the *dharmakāya* Buddha as one's father and mother.
Regarding the various joys and sufferings of the true retribution in other realms and this world, one may partially realize them by pouring forth the heart;
yet ultimately, not even a single hair’s breadth deviates from the ultimate principle. For this reason, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas thoroughly understand [this].
The two realms of suffering and pleasure are proclaimed as the gateway for adoption and rejection. May all sentient beings take refuge in the Path of Rectitude;
this is the Dharma by which the World-Honored One draws beings upward. Therefore, wise Mahāsattvas spend their entire lives recollecting the Buddha and sit facing west.
Su Dongpo habitually carried the "Official Passport to the West" and an image of Amitābha Buddha; these were all means of taking refuge.

Regarding the mind of ultimate bliss: if people today wish to seek the method for casting off suffering, they must rely on the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation), which can eliminate the sufferings of ten thousand kalpas and serves as the swift path for returning to that land.
When one reaches the state where suffering is realized as empty, one perceives that self-nature (*svabhāva*) is untainted; thus, there is no meaning of "suffering.
Since self-nature is eternally pure, there is no meaning of "bliss. To realize this non-duality—*amala-vijñāna*—is the true essence of the Pure Land.

There is no meaning of suffering and no absence of joy. When one attains the realization of the meaning of ultimate bliss (*sukhāvatī*), one knows that in that land there are no manifold sufferings, but only the reception of various joys.
Because it possesses such spontaneous joy, it is named "Ultimate Bliss. This is the mind of the Bodhisattva.
If people were to know this as I know it, would they not be joyful? If people were not to know this as I do not know it, would they not be pained?
Therefore, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for sentient beings submerged in the ocean of suffering, gave rise to this urgent concern marked by knit brows;
he did not begrudge the disorder of his own state to bestow upon them the bliss of Ultimate Joy, surpassing the toil of the hells.
People today should reflect upon the world: for the kindness of even a single garment or a single meal, one must surely think of repaying it.

Since the Buddha possesses such a heart of profound compassion, how could one possibly disobey his command? If one does not believe the Buddha’s words, what words can be trusted? One will then fail to be born in the Pure Land.
In which lands can one be born?
Furthermore, it is said that there are three calamities: first, the kalpa of famine; second, the kalpa of pestilence; and third, the kalpa of weapons.

Furthermore, it is said that the eight difficulties (aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ) are: hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, being blind or deaf, being mute or speech-impaired, having no eloquence or intelligence, living before or after a Buddha, and being born in the northern continent of Uttarakuru.
△ Detailed Description of the Exquisite Realm:
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Land of Ultimate Bliss has sevenfold railings, sevenfold jeweled nets, and sevenfold rows of trees.
All are surrounded on all sides by the four precious gems;

this specifically clarifies the matters of pleasure. The railings encircle the exterior of the trees: those that run horizontally are called "lans" (rails), and those that stand vertically are called "shun" (balusters).
The nets cover the tops of the trees, layered one above another in seven tiers. [They are made of] the four precious gems.
These are the first four of the seven treasures: namely, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
These four treasures subsequently manifest three more treasures, together forming seven. "Pervading" (*zhōuzào*) means to fill completely; "surrounding" (*wéirào*) means to encircle and protect.
The railings and nets are all composed of these four treasures, and are all produced from the merits of Amitābha Buddha’s myriad practices.
This is the adornment of accomplishment. As for the "rows of trees," they form successive lines without any disorder.
Regarding the "sevenfold" [enclosures], each single layer of railings surrounds a single row of trees; thus, it is said that they alternate layer by layer.
Compared to this land, things such as flowering and fruit-bearing trees, as well as stones, are scattered and inconsistent; they merely alternate between flourishing and withering.
The adornments of that land are composed entirely of pure jewels; they have been thus from antiquity to the present.

The light of the long sun shines with radiant splendor, covering the trees, forests, flowers, and fruits. Sandalwood fragrance trees and auspicious fruit trees—various named trees—are arranged in rows surrounding it.
Although it is said there are seven layers, this is merely a general description of these adornments, which fill the entire world.
They are beyond measure. Row upon row they stand straight; stem upon stem they face one another; branch upon branch they are aligned;

leaf upon leaf they turn toward each other; flower upon flower they harmonize; fruit upon fruit they correspond. All their golden roots and golden stems, as well as their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, are likewise made of gold.
There are also some with golden roots and silver leaves, where the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are likewise divided between gold and silver. Thus it is.
These alternating features are called the Three Jewels. As they increase and multiply, they are known as the seven [rows].
As for the walking trees, they are composed of the seven precious substances. Each tree is eight thousand yojanas high. Each flower and leaf displays the radiant colors of various jewels:
from within the lapis lazuli color, golden light emanates; from within the crystal color, crimson light emanates.
Thus, the radiance of these forms is brilliantly magnificent and inexhaustible.
Each tree has seven layers of nets, and within each net there are five hundred *koṭis* of exquisite flower-palaces, like the palaces of Brahmā. Divine youths dwell therein.
Each leaf of the trees is exactly twenty-five *yojanas* in length and breadth; the leaves possess a thousand colors.

Within it are various exquisite flowers, the color of Jambūnada gold. Amidst these revolving flowers, various fruits emerge like the *śakra-ghaṭa* (Indra’s vase), emitting great radiance that transforms into banners, streamers, and immeasurable jeweled canopies.
Within these jeweled canopies, all the Buddha-activities of the trichiliocosm are reflected; therein appears Amitābha.
In the lecture halls and the residences of the arhats, there are ponds made of the seven treasures within each, and trees made of the seven treasures without.
These trees constantly emit extraordinary fragrances that pervade the worlds of the ten directions.

All sentient beings who smell them give rise to joy and together resolve their minds upon the Way, just as the sentient beings of this land feel when they hear of the wonders of those sublime realms. It is just like this.

It is as if one has heard of the scent of extraordinary incense. When the sentient beings of this land encounter auspicious gatherings or sights such as decorated pavilions, they invariably go to view them;
they should likewise gaze upon these sublime scenes of the West. Yet, why is it that people alone do not delight in following [this path]?
Recently, someone asked: "The Way of the Sages cuts off greed and desire, so that all forms and appearances are rendered empty."
"There is no distinction between 'that' and 'I. Why, then, should one seek pleasure? He replied, "These words are most consistent with reason; they are indeed the holy path.
[The master] then asked him, "Suppose you were to encounter gold and jade on the road; would you truly be able to disregard them completely?
If you have not yet broken through this barrier, how can you claim to be free from desire? Such is the nature of the mind of craving."
One will suffer delusion for a lifetime. For instance, even if a window paper is slightly torn by someone, one still feels anger;
even if a single needle is taken away by someone, one still feels stinginess; and though the storehouses are full, the mind remains unsatisfied.
If even a single servant has not returned, one already grieves over their loss; every glance and every step is nothing but attachment.
Once the great time limit arrives, even one's own body becomes a discarded thing—how much more so external objects?
Reflecting on this with a quiet mind, it is as if one were in a dream. Why not uphold this path of mindfulness of the Buddha and seek rebirth in that land? This is indeed...
The method for reviving the dead from the grave, although it still relies upon desire as its means, does not involve attachment to impermanent things outside of oneself;
rather, one contemplates only the Buddha’s radiance illuminating all, gathering everything into the realm of sublime adornment.
This is the conduct naturally appropriate for one who wishes to bid eternal farewell to saṃsāra. Unless one recognizes this path in advance, when the eyes close in the future, toward—
Where shall we stay for the night?
Furthermore, it was said that this land uses the *zhang* and *chi* as its standard measurements, whereas that land uses the *yojana* as its unit of calculation.
As for the *yojana*, there are distinctions between large and small; sometimes fifteen *li* constitute one *yojana*, and sometimes forty *li* do.
One *yojana* is what is called a small *yojana*. This is divided into three grades:
a medium *yojana* is sixty *li*, and a large *yojana* is eighty *li*.

It is further stated that there are four great continents (*caturmahādvīpa*) and a multitude of worlds where Brahmā kings reside; one thousand of these is called a small chiliocosm (*sāhasracūdikalokadhātu*).

One thousand times a small chiliocosm constitutes a medium chiliocosm (*dvisāhasramadhyamalokadhātu*). One thousand times a medium chiliocosm constitutes a great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*). Taken together, this is termed a "trichiliocosm of three thousandfold world systems."
Furthermore, it is said that the trees of the seven treasures are: first, shame (hrī); second, remorse (apatrāpya); third, faith (śraddhā); fourth, precept-keeping (śīla);
fifth, learning (śruta); sixth, relinquishment (tyāga); and seventh, wisdom (prajñā).
△ First, it is concluded as "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī).
For this reason, that land is named Ultimate Bliss.
This statement concludes what precedes and responds to what follows. It is because of the railings, rows of trees, and the successive layers of pure worlds [that it is so named].
This is called the Pure Land. Within these clusters of jade trees and fragrant groves, there is no suffering; one experiences only various joys. This is named "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī).
To examine this meaning thoroughly, it is entirely contained within what has been expressed in the preceding text. Why, then, does the Buddha again bring up Ultimate Bliss?
It is because he fears that people may know only of the wondrous realm of Ultimate Bliss, yet remain unaware of its railings and enclosures.
As for the origin of the rows of trees, one further phrase is added to clarify that the myriad virtues of the self-nature are both vertical and horizontal;
these are called "balustrades. That the self-nature encompasses the Dharma-realm is called "lattices. That the self-nature nurtures all manner of goodness is called "rows of trees.
Thus, one understands the meaning of this sublime realm: it arises from the virtuous conduct perfected upon the basis of the self-nature. Now, since...
The meaning of the objective realm (*viṣaya*) is as follows. Every single sentient being among the great masses can establish for themselves a supreme realm of Sukhāvatī.
Although they may understand this and penetrate it, I fear that each person has not yet been willing to resolve their mind to lay the foundation.

As for those who are truly able to resolve their minds, they are like the Venerable Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu during the Jin Dynasty, who for thirty years did not set foot inside the marketplace. His mind—

While single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha, he suddenly entered a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). There he beheld Amitābha Buddha, with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta attending and following him on his left and right.
A compassionate light covered the Master’s head. He then looked toward the four directions and saw railings, flower canopies, and various kinds of adornments—a pure and sublime realm.
Furthermore, he saw immeasurable transformation Buddhas expounding the wondrous Dharma. The Buddhas said, "We..."

Having reached this point, he comforted his mind, saying, "In seven days, you shall be born in my land. When the time arrived, the Master again saw the Buddha coming to welcome him, whereupon he sat down and passed away.
Furthermore, during the Song dynasty, there was the Grand Officer Zhongli Jingrong, who renounced worldly glory to dwell in a thatched hut and practice the recitation of the Buddha's name.
He vowed to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). When someone asked him, "The West is an exceedingly distant place; how can one possibly reach it?

he replied, "You do not know that the West is right here within your own home. Several years later, the Great Official beheld the Buddha manifesting the Land of Ultimate Bliss and returned to the West together with the Buddha. Those of today who wish to be companions of those ancients should likewise aspire to this.
If you immediately follow this ritual to arouse such a resolve, holding fast to a single Buddha-name with ten thousand minds unified as one,
never regressing, then not only will your merit and wisdom be fully perfected, but even if the Buddhas come to welcome and lead you, they shall not be able to push you out of the Western Land.
△ Displaying the pond waters.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, in the land of Ultimate Bliss, there are ponds made of the seven treasures, filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities.
The bottom of the ponds is entirely covered with ground of golden sand.
Furthermore, as stated above, within the Land of Ultimate Bliss there are ponds made of the seven treasures;

these ponds contain water of eight meritorious qualities, and each pond has its bottom entirely strewn with golden sand. The pure water is deep and full, wherein one may bathe and become free from defilement.
As for the people and the ponds, there are also large and small ones arranged to the left and right.
Some are ten yojanas wide, some twenty, thirty, or even up to a hundred thousand yojanas, resembling the great ocean.
Each pond is composed of the seven precious jewels. While these earthly ponds are constructed of earth and stone, those in that land are not so; they are made of jewels.
It is naturally and spontaneously formed. As for the seven treasures, they are the precious trees produced by the King of Wish-Fulfilling Jewels (*cintāmaṇi-rāja*).
This King of Jewels is named the Mind-King (*citta-rāja*). The trees branch into fourteen limbs, each emitting immeasurable, wondrous colors of the seven treasures.
The channels are made of yellow gold, and beneath these channels, five-colored jewel-light is constantly emitted. The bottom is composed of diamond sand within a golden pond.
In some, the bottom consists of white silver sand; in the crystal ponds, the bottom consists of amber sand. The sands of all these ponds are distinct from one another.
As for what is called the water of eight virtues, it likewise flows forth from the seven treasures.
As for the water of eight virtues: first, the virtue of clarity; second, the virtue of purity;
third, the virtue of sweetness; fourth, the virtue of lightness and softness; fifth, the virtue of moisture and luster; sixth, the virtue of tranquility and harmony;
seventh, the virtue of removing hunger and thirst; and eighth, the virtue of nourishing the roots of goodness. The pond contains this water of eight virtues.
To benefit sentient beings, there exists such a precious bathing pool of benefit. Why not descend into the pool for a bath?
By doing so, one will immediately be liberated from birth and death, all karmic obstacles, and suffering; even King Yama shall be unable to do you harm.
During the Song dynasty, there was a man from Yuhang who was the Chan Master Yongming Shou of Jingci Temple in Hangzhou; throughout his life, he was diligent in transforming others.
He practiced the path of mindfulness of the Buddha and the liberation of living beings, thereby attaining rebirth in the highest grade of the highest level at the stage of fruition.

Later, there was a monk who specifically circumambulated the master’s stupa and paid homage with sincere reverence. When people asked him why, he replied: "In the past, when I was ill, I entered the underworld.
I saw the image of a monk enshrined to the left of the hall, to whom the King burned incense and prostrated. I asked the underworld official for the reason, and the official said: 'This..."
This refers to Chan Master Yongming of Jingci, a high monk of the Pure Land school who attained the highest grade of rebirth in the Pure Land.

Even the King of the Underworld respected him; it was not only those with pure karma who were reborn there, for even those who were reborn while still carrying their karmic burdens could not easily be summoned by the underworld authorities.
As it is said, the merit of reciting the Buddha’s name is like the blessing of a single bath; one must not fail to focus one's will solely on the practice of nianfo.
This is simply because one is addicted to the worldly illness of defilement, craving form and greedily clinging to life.
One fails to realize that form is but a phantom film before the eye, and that birth is like a bubble upon the water—driven by the wind and chasing the waves, vanishing in an instant.

With this ignorance, one remains deluded and obscured for a lifetime; unless one washes the heart and cleanses the defilements to seek rebirth in the Buddha-land, it is like a long-term traveler in a foreign land.
I constantly fail to think of returning [to the path], and I wish to endure a life lived in vain and a death met by chance; how can my folly reach such a point?
Nevertheless, if this body does not attain deliverance in this present life, toward what other life shall I turn to deliver it?
△ Manifesting the terraces and pavilions:
the stairways on all four sides are composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Above them are multi-storied pavilions, likewise made of gold and silver.
It is adorned with lapis lazuli, crystal, mother-of-pearl, red pearls, and agate. Regarding the four sides:
there is a pool of water in the center, and its surrounding four sides serve as stairways. That which is detached from the ground is called a "stair" (kai).
The level path is called the Way (*mārga*). It is composed entirely of four precious substances as its ground, adorned with exquisite beauty and purity beyond compare.
Upon this ground, there are further three treasures—namely, *śaṅkha* (conch), *lohitamukti* (red pearl), and *musāragalva* (agate)—which together constitute the seven treasures.
From within each of these treasures, immeasurable rays of light emerge; these lights are like flowers, merging together into one.
The Radiant Terrace. Upon this terrace are tiered pavilions, all adorned and fashioned from a hundred jewels.
Within are Amitābha Buddha, lecture halls, monasteries, official palaces, and Brahma temples, beyond counting.

The adornment of these pure realms and monasteries surpasses the celestial palaces inhabited by the Heavenly Emperor by hundreds of thousands of millions of times; such is the dwelling place of the Bodhisattvas.
It is likewise so for the palaces and towers of the devas and humans; some are composed of one kind of jewel, two kinds of jewels, or even up to immeasurable jewels.
These are arranged in various tiers, encircling the four quarters, with railings, nets, and necklaces densely covering them above.
Every tower, pavilion, and palace possesses its own flower canopies, banners, curtains, and celestial music.
A gentle breeze stirred them, causing all to produce pure sounds that expounded the dharmas of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.
These pavilions were magnificent and sublime, vast and lofty according to one's wishes, floating in mid-air with both interior and exterior clearly transparent.
There are those who have transcended the dust and defilements of the mundane world yet remain upon this earth; this is due to the varying degrees of depth in their cultivation while seeking the Way.

If all sentient beings of the great earth were willing to lean against the door, snap their fingers, and enter within, they would immediately know that in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas proclaim the Dharma with the blazing radiance of their own inherent nature—not only...

One who thoroughly understands the supreme realm has already entered the Buddha’s tower. Nevertheless, while it is easy to swing open the gates of the Buddha-dharma, I fear that people will not believe the Buddha’s words and will have no desire to see the Buddha.
If they do wish to see the Buddha, let them take their own mind as the gate.
Take the Buddha’s name as the finger; exert yourself and practice it day and night, making it the rule to strike [the lute] until it opens.

Only then will you come to know the principle of the profound source of the successive pavilions and towers. Someone asked: "A renunciant has forgotten purity and defilement in their mind and does not crave splendor or beauty.
For what reason, then, does the Buddha speak of adorning worlds and cause people to seek rebirth there? Does this not inevitably conflict with the Way?"
"Yes. He replied, "If you say this is merely a matter of oral samādhi, what is there to find difficult about it?
Let me ask you: would you be willing to make a latrine your permanent residence? Would you be willing to eat and drink from the same trough as dogs, pigs, oxen, and horses?
Would you be willing to sleep together with putrid corpses? Would you be willing to dwell amidst the pus, blood, excrement, and urine of those afflicted with various foul diseases?"
Has this been so for months and years? Regarding these several points, you have been joyful and at ease, showing no concern whatsoever; thus, you permit me to speak a bold word.

I, too, love to hear it. If, however, there are things externally difficult to endure or internally giving rise to doubt and resentment, then the distinction between the pure and the defiled has not yet been emptied, and feelings of hatred and attachment still remain. Yet you proceed to discourse loftily of the Great Sage.

To deny the existence of the Buddha-lands and regard rebirth there with utter contempt can be called nothing less than deceiving Heaven and deluding men. They fail to realize that the Buddha’s grace is vast and profound;

he intentionally accommodates those of dull faculties and ordinary capacity by clearly demonstrating the nature of suffering and bliss, so that people may rejoice in the former and loathe the latter, thereby becoming able to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
This is like first using a hook to draw them in, and subsequently leading them into the Buddha’s wisdom—a metaphor for this very process.
It is like a country currently suffering from famine and cold suddenly hearing of a land of plenty and warmth; or like one constantly dwelling on a dark precipice suddenly beholding a realm of light.
How could one’s body and mind not leap for joy, abandoning the old to seek the new?
Once rebirth is attained, liberation will ultimately be achieved. One should contemplate the skillful means of being welcomed and guided in this manner.
△ A lotus flower appears before him.
Within the pond, there is a lotus flower as large as a chariot wheel; it is blue with a blue radiance, yellow with a yellow radiance, and red with a red radiance.
White in color, with white light, subtle and pure in fragrance.
The previous mention was of the exterior of the pond; the present description refers to within the pond. "Lotus" (*padma*) is the general name.
When it has not yet opened, it is collectively called *kumuda*; when it is about to fall, it is collectively called *kamala*. The four types listed below are all the primary varieties.
These are the names of [lotuses] when they bloom. First is *puṇḍarīka*, which refers to the white lotus.
Second is *utpala*, which refers to the blue lotus. Third is *padma*, which refers to the red lotus. Fourth is *kumuda*, which refers to the yellow lotus.
Regarding "as large as a chariot wheel," this compares their size to a chariot wheel; the size is measured according to the standard of a chariot wheel.
One yojana. However, these lotus flowers have no fixed number; each appears according to the capacity of beings.
Although they are compared to chariot wheels, this is merely a conventional approximation of their size. Within each pond there are sixty billion lotus flowers made of the seven precious gems.
Their circular dimensions vary in size, ranging from one or two yojanas up to even hundreds of thousands of yojanas. These are the lotuses.
The flowers spread throughout the world. Each precious lotus has immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of petals.
Those that are blue emit blue light; those that are white emit white light; and those that are azure, yellow, crimson, or purple likewise emit their respective lights.
From each flower issue forth immeasurable colors, immeasurable lights, and immeasurable Buddhas. Each Buddha radiates immeasurable rays of light, [teaching] through the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
Within it, immeasurable dharmas are taught. May all sentient beings together emerge from the wheel of suffering. Someone may ask:
"If a single Buddha is sufficient to deliver beings, why rely on so many Buddhas to mutually protect and save sentient beings? The answer is:
Amitābha Buddha. Because he made vows while on the stage of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), his merit was vast and great;

thus, he accomplished a supreme realm that is immeasurable and boundless, resulting in the inexhaustible manifestation of lotus flowers. All of these arise from the single Buddha Amitābha, appearing through the self-nature radiance (*svabhāva-prabhāsvara*).
Therefore, it is said that the lotuses are subtle, wondrous, fragrant, and pure. Although there is a multitude of Buddhas, they are in fact one Buddha. Thus it is said in the world:
The Venerable One’s comparison of the wheel to the lotus is because the lotus also contains the function of the wheel.

In this land, one revolves within saṃsāra, with birth and death never ceasing; in that land, one is born through transformation within a lotus, which is precisely the cessation of the revolutions of saṃsāra.
If a person recites the Buddha’s name from the very beginning of their resolve, they shall immediately be born upon a lotus in the Western Land, thereby establishing the foundation.

As for the name: the more one contemplates, the longer it endures, until the fruit of buddha-remembrance ripens and the person proceeds to that lotus to be born there by transformation within a lotus flower.
If one withdraws midway and thoughts of cessation arise, the lotus will half-wither; if one withdraws entirely, the lotus will perish.
The metaphor of the lotus resembles the image of a chariot wheel. Furthermore, the body of the Buddha-Sage is like a lotus.
Pure, unobstructed, and free from hindrance, although lotuses appear in profusion, they ultimately manifest the true principle.
This is precisely the function of the Buddha’s Samādhi of Quiescent Light; thus, the lotus can carry people, and people can produce lotuses.

Like a ferryboat, the lotus receives and guides those sentient beings who practice *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation), leading them back to Sukhāvatī. To traverse the three realms in a mere moment—how could this compare to worldly things?
To the south lies Mount Tiantai; to the north, Mount Wutai. Amidst myriad labors and hardships, if one can board this precious vessel, the entire world is but a single glance away.
Why not do so? To board that vessel, one need only single-mindedly hold fast to a single phrase of the Buddha’s name.
Even if there were fiery wheels or sharp swords, approaching them would not heal [the pain], nor would touching them cause injury;
one will naturally and before long attain Buddhahood. This is what is meant by "a single hero supporting the heads of ten thousand people. Do not fear difficulties.

Formerly, there was a man from Dongping Prefecture named Gao Haoxiang; upon reading the *Amitābha Sūtra* for three days, he immediately entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and became self-aware.
Her body floated amidst a pond of radiant lotuses. In a short while, she ascended a lotus flower to pay homage to the Buddha, from whom she beheld his golden countenance, its brilliance shining afar.
Three days after this event, a wondrous fragrance filled her chamber; the Buddha had come to welcome her to the highest grade of the upper birth.
Furthermore, there was a woman named Huang of Siming who lost her husband early in life; she resolved her mind to recite the Buddha’s name, and at the moment of death, she saw the Buddha arrive.
She welcomed [the Buddha] and took her leave of the assembly before passing away. After her death, a single lotus flower sprang from the ground; thus she was called the Lotus Maiden (*Padmāvatī*).

One can see how easy it was for the ancients to achieve such a state, and one may likewise take them as a model. Someone asked: "Regarding the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) in the present age..."

There are not a few such people. Why is it that they do not see their attainment of Buddhahood? The answer is: It is because, on the whole, their minds of half-belief and half-doubt cause harm that is no slight matter.
If a person does not wish to undergo this harm of doubt, then they should recite the Buddha’s name with every thought.
Disregarding all peril and ruin, one proceeds straight ahead like a swift horse being spurred on.

If one maintains such mindfulness without forgetting, and after a long time the mind of mindfulness remains unchanged, then one will know that every head is a pure land and every place a realm of lotuses.
Only then will one believe that water flowing from the side of a rock is cold, and that wind coming from within a flower is fragrant.
△ Second, the summary of the realm of Ultimate Bliss:

Śāriputra, the land of Ultimate Bliss is adorned with such meritorious qualities as the aforementioned railings, ponds, pavilions, and lotus flowers. All these various adornments are due to the causal power of Amitābha Buddha.
The great vows made therein, as well as the great practices cultivated following those vows, achieve immeasurable sublime realms through immeasurable merit.
It is essential that vows give rise to practice, and practice fulfills vows; there is no exception to this throughout the Bodhisattva’s causal stage.
Only when practice is perfected and vows fulfilled does one attain the Buddha-way. The vows he undertook were precisely the forty-eight.
This is the vow. It should be recorded in its entirety; however, fearing that it might appear tedious to the reader, I have briefly compiled several key points.

To grasp the general meaning, one may infer the Buddha’s vow as follows: "When I become a Buddha, within my land there shall be no hells, hungry ghosts, birds, or beasts, nor any creatures that crawl, fly, or wriggle. If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha."
Furthermore, he made this vow: "When I become a Buddha, may all those in my land be entirely free from lustful indulgence, anger, and delusion.
If I do not attain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha."
Furthermore, his vow says: "When I become a Buddha, let there not even be the name of 'unwholesome' heard among the people of my land, much less its actual existence.
If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha."
Furthermore, his vow says: "When I become a Buddha, may the people in my land realize that the body is an illusion and possess no mind of greedy attachment;
if I do not attain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha."
Furthermore, he made this vow: "When I become a Buddha, may all those born in my land be born by transformation from lotus flowers within ponds of the seven treasures.
If I do not attain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha."

Furthermore, his vow says: "When I become a Buddha, within my buddha-field, from the ground upward to the void of space, there shall be palaces and towers, ponds, streams, and flowering trees, all fashioned from immeasurable varieties of jewels and hundreds of thousands of kinds of incense."
If these [vows] are not collectively fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.
Furthermore, he made this vow: "When I attain Buddhahood, may all manner of ornamental adornments pervade the entire land, and for all sentient beings..."
He is able to expound [the Dharma] in its entirety. This constitutes the Great Vow of practicing what one preaches to deliver others. Without attaining this vow, he shall never become a Buddha.
Having made this vow, he abides in true wisdom and cultivates the practices of a bodhisattva.

Throughout immeasurable kalpas, he teaches and transforms others with a mind of diligent perseverance, so that all sentient beings within those immeasurable kalpas may give rise to the aspiration for the Way and enter the rank of Buddhahood together.
Only now has the fulfillment of the great vow been attained. It is not only Amitābha Buddha who possesses this great vow;

likewise, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas equally possess these practices and vows, universally acting for the sake of sentient beings to rescue them from suffering and distress.
Furthermore, the celestial immortals, sages, and deities also possess a thousandfold of earnest exhortations.
All hope that sentient beings will become good people; there is no mention of "loving views" (*priyadṛṣṭi*) or the sufferings of the "mountain of knives and trees of swords.

Someone asked: "The Buddha must surely feel deep compassion for the suffering of sentient beings; is this not perhaps excessive concern? He replied: "It is not that the Buddha seeks to do something for his own sake.
It is as Confucius said: 'Is it not the very root of benevolence (*ren*)? This is precisely the same with the Buddha."
So may it be. Inferring from this intent, it is but natural for people of the world to turn toward the good and draw near to the worthy;

since such conduct is already established, what need is there for further detailed discussion? I merely revere the instruction of Master Lianchi, who said: "Impermanence is swift; single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name.
If one can truly achieve this single-mindedness, then the compassionate efforts of the Buddhas and Sages will find their fulfillment in every aspiration.
△ First, the celestial hosts are shown.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, in that Buddha-land, celestial music is constantly played.
While the preceding passage described the jeweled ponds, this speaks of the golden ground above, where flowers and music shine together in splendor. All these celestial sounds...

I have heard that when Arhats make offerings to the Buddhas, they do not use ordinary objects; rather, they employ hundreds of thousands of fragrant flowers and hundreds of thousands of musical performances, each vying with the other in excellence.
These are all spontaneous musical performances, none of which are not the sound of the Dharma. They are pure, resonant, and far-reaching;
subtle, wondrous, brilliant, and elegant, such that no other sounds can equal them. They cannot be compared to worldly pleasures.
It is the celestial music of Heaven; it is not a sound produced by striking. Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says that the celestial drums resound of their own accord.
Now, since the physical forms of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are all empty, for what purpose do one offer incense, flowers, and musical performances as offerings? What is the underlying meaning?
It is because Amitābha’s Way is lofty and his virtue is profound, and his bestowal of grace is vast, that he moves the sounds of the various devas.

I have heard that by constantly scattering such incense, flowers, and music throughout the Buddha-fields, one performs the most supreme form of veneration and praise, for it is never forgotten for even a moment.
