Thus, when people of today recollect the Buddha at the time of their death, they obtain celestial music to welcome them from the sky.
This shows that the Buddha values people; one can thus know that the Pure Land constantly produces celestial music, and this fact is not false.
△ Next, to clarify the golden ground:
the ground is made of yellow gold.

This follows the principle of the former giving rise to the latter. That is to say, in the world of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), above there is the joy of the heavens, and below the ground is adorned with gold.

What is called the "Golden Ground" is a ground composed of a hundred jewels, serving as a ground of lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*) that radiates light throughout the great trichiliocosm. As for the "gold," it is the adornment of the ground's surface; its light...
They also shone brilliantly; the two lights merged together in a splendor so profound it could not be fathomed. Thus, the Buddha praised and extolled the golden ground.
Not only did they hear celestial music with their ears, but they also beheld celestial flowers with their eyes. Pure and translucent both within and without, it transcended the ten directions.
Furthermore, one perceives subtle, exquisite, and pure fragrances, which sweetly nourish the true nature (*tianzhen*). Someone may ask:
"For what reason is gold considered the most precious in the Buddha-lands? The answer is: Gold represents the equality of the *tathatā* (suchness) of self-nature.
This *tathatā* is unmixed and undefiled; it is unchanging and immutable. It remains ever-new throughout ten thousand kalpas. As for equality:
Neither increasing nor decreasing, neither high nor low, it is the principle realized by the thousand sages; this is the meaning of "nature" (*dhātu*). The meaning of nature is illustrated by gold:
gold is hidden within the earth, and the earth gives birth to gold. Once the earth is excavated, the pure gold remains unchanged in its color even after being smelted and cast a thousand times.
Therefore, gold is used as a metaphor for the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), which remains ever-new throughout ten thousand kalpas. The Buddha-nature...
It is likened to gold, which remains uncorrupted throughout the ages. Although it is called "Golden Land," it is in fact the "Ground of Nature" (Svabhāva-bhūmi). Again, he asked:
"Since the Buddhas of antiquity have no dwelling or attachment in their minds, for what reason do they cause people to seek birth in a Buddha-land, specifically designating the West?
He replied: "This is a question concerning the ultimate principle. In the Mahayana, the minds of all Buddhas have no desires; thus, there is no..."
This is the mind that guards the corners [of propriety]. Therefore, the Buddha said: "High mountains and level plains are all Pure Land;
the West is this very land, and this land is the West. There is nowhere that is not the Tathāgata’s site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

It can be seen that the Buddhas and Sages originally have no dwelling place in the West; it is simply because the Buddha-nature is like gold, and gold belongs to the West—this is merely a metaphorical concession to the Buddha.

The direction of the West signifies the stage of indestructibility. Furthermore, for those ordinary beings of dull faculties, it is necessary to point toward a specific direction so that they may gain confidence in their reliance upon it and cultivate the path to awakening.

Moreover, since the site of Śrāvastī actually lies in the west, it is precisely because the provisional leads to the realization of the ultimate that I exhort all people in this world to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and awaken.

The Amitābha of intrinsic nature immediately enters the stream of the Buddhas. Although there is no principle that one must necessarily go to the Western Land, once one has reached the West, those who do not believe in the Pure Land simply have no aspiration to go because they do not know the benefit of relying upon its actual efficacy.
It is like a person traveling to a distant marketplace who must first seek out a place to stay.
Only then do they attend to their affairs. When evening falls and it becomes dark, they have a place to lodge.
To seek out a lodging beforehand is what is meant by "cultivating the Pure Land. When evening falls and it becomes dark refers to the arrival of the great deadline [of death].
Having a place to lodge refers to being born within a lotus flower and not falling into the evil realms. This is what is called "mindfulness."
For those who seek rebirth in that land, it is truly for their own secure settlement—the destination they reach after closing their eyes in death.
Were it otherwise, they would be trampling upon themselves; would this not be painful? Those who wish to be born in that realm must earnestly emulate and learn from his example.
For sixty years, the layman Wang Longshu of the Song dynasty abstained from killing and practiced the release of living beings, wearing simple cloth garments and subsisting on vegetables.
While eating, he single-mindedly recited the Buddha’s name. One day, he suddenly called out the Buddha’s name in a loud voice and declared, "The Buddha has come to welcome me.
He then stood upright and passed away, his body as rigid as a planted tree. The people of that land all saw two youths dressed in blue robes.

Carrying banners, they led the Master westward; every household provided for his needs. If people today wish to follow his Dharma and aspire toward the ancients, do not harbor even the slightest doubt or confusion.
△ Next, it is shown that the heavens rain exquisite flowers.
Throughout the six periods of day and night, they rain *mandārava* flowers.
The previous mention of "golden ground" now signifies the constant raining of celestial flowers. "Raining" refers to praising the Buddha’s virtues and bringing benefit.
It is the rain of the Dharma for all sentient beings. As for the celestial flowers, they follow fixed seasonal patterns just as in this land:
the sun and moon revolve around Mount Sumeru, thereby dividing day and night. When it is midday in Jambudvīpa in the south, it is midnight in Uttarakuru in the north;
when the sun sets in Pūrvavideha in the east, it rises in Aparagoyānī in the west. Thus the sun and moon alternate their course.
As they approach, there is a distinction between near and far; thus, the increase and decrease of day and night are not fixed.

In the World of Ultimate Bliss, day and night are distinguished solely by the *mandārava* flower. This flower is called a "celestial flower," and that land has no four seasons, nor does it experience cold or heat.
It is eternally bright and never dark; day and night are indistinguishable. [This is known] by the singing of birds and the blooming of flowers.
The blossoming [of the flowers] is the dawn; their closing and the birds' settling upon them is night. The opening of one petal constitutes one period (*kāla*);

when they have opened to six petals, it is one day. The shedding of one petal constitutes one period; when they have shed down to six petals, it is one night. Day and night thus remain without increase or decrease;
hence it is said that there are six periods in a day and night. As for the "celestial flowers," they descend from the heavens. Although...
It is called "Celestial Flowers. In reality, they are flowers from trees; there are many such trees. When the wind rises and carries the flowers, they emit extraordinary fragrances.
Furthermore, five hundred kinds of pure and elegant sounds follow the wind in all directions, making offerings to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the great assembly of Śrāvakas.
As the flowers fall upon that ground, they accumulate to the height of inches and feet, brilliant and beautiful as far as the eye can see, with a fragrance beyond compare.
If driven by turbulent winds, they scatter and fall in all directions; such is not the case for the radiance of the Buddha-fields, which never fails to be thus.
Someone may ask: "How do these flowers descend from heaven? The answer is: "The celestial flowers are the very nature of the Buddha's wisdom and the descent of his virtuous conduct.
If a person cultivates and attains the Way, their spiritual power will become pervasive and their strength [will manifest]."
The ability to manifest such flowers is likewise so. Thus it is said that when the self-nature is in delusion, it is like a flower still in its bud;

when one suddenly awakens to the self-nature, it is like a flower in full bloom. If sentient beings desire to see these celestial flowers, they should focus their minds on the Buddha with single-minded devotion.

After a long time, a sublime realm will naturally appear before them. Only then will they believe that the Dharma is not empty or deceptive. This occurs without having undergone bitter toil or ascetic practices.
Previously, do not say that the Buddha-dharma is like a pavilion in the air.

If you utter such words, you will not only slander the Triple Gem, but will also create for yourself the three karmas of body, speech, and mind in their entirety. You should know that a sutra says: there was once a śrāmaṇera.
He laughed lightly at an old bhikṣu whose recitation of the sūtras sounded like the barking of a dog. This old bhikṣu was an arhat;
because he had instructed a śrāmaṇera to go quickly and seek repentance, the man narrowly escaped hell. Otherwise, he would have fallen into the body of a dog.
Such is the harm caused by a single malicious laugh. Therefore, it is said that one who fears the words of the Sage will remain so until the end of their life.
"Treasure" refers to being moistened by the rain of the Dharma. To resolve to recite the Buddha’s name is never to have one's hopes in vain.

△ Holding these to offer as an act of worship, the sentient beings of that land always at the clear dawn each take a robe-sack filled with various wonderful flowers to make offerings to those in other directions.
At the time of the morning meal, the ten trillion Buddhas return to their respective lands to eat, sit in meditation, and perform walking meditation.
The phrase "celestial flowers" refers to sentient beings taking them to offer to the Buddhas. Regarding "sentient beings," this excludes the Buddhas;
it refers to those from the bodhisattvas downward who are reborn in that land, as both the great assembly and ordinary worldlings are termed "sentient beings. This occurs at the hour of early dawn.
This refers to the foremost of the six periods [of the day]. The mind at the first period is most upright and pure; therefore, it is called the "clear and tranquil mind.
When sentient beings constantly use a robe-sack (*niku*) to hold flowers and offer them to the Buddha at dawn, they take the time of offering as primary, so that their minds become upright and pure.
This serves to manifest the utmost reverence of the very beginning. A "robe-sack" is a vessel for holding flowers. As for "wondrous flowers":

To say "heavenly flowers" refers to those offered to ten trillion Buddhas; to say "in all places throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions" means that he is able to make offerings everywhere to all Buddhas at once. "At mealtime" refers to the morning meal.
Even during this brief period of mealtime, he makes offerings to so many Buddhas and returns to his own land. Furthermore—
Regarding the phrase "at the time of eating," it refers to its swiftness. That all Bodhisattvas possess such power is due to the original vow of Amitābha Buddha, which states:
"When sentient beings are reborn in my land, they shall all attain the supernormal power of psychic travel (*ṛddhi-pāda*), the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), and the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*)."
His mind is all-pervasive and complete in every respect. In the span of a single thought-moment, he traverses hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddha-lands.
His practice accords with his cultivation, and his cultivation accords with his practice. As for the Buddha’s eating: it is called "food" because it nurtures and sustains the myriad virtues.
When it is said that he eats at mealtime, this is a metaphor for the duration of a single meal; yet, as his activities are already all-encompassing, one may still say that he eats.
This is not the eating of food. As for the passage below concerning "eating and walking," it means that sentient beings turn back upon themselves to eat, and having eaten, they walk.
At the time of eating, silver bowls, golden bowls, and bowls made of various jewels appear before them at will;
within them, food and drink of a hundred flavors are filled to the brim—sour, salty, sweet, and bland—each according to their wishes, with nothing lacking.

It is never lacking; once consumed, it digests of itself without leaving any residue. Sometimes, upon seeing a form or smelling a fragrance, they perceive it as food and naturally become satiated and comfortable, without any attachment to its flavor.
Their bodies and minds become light and agile. Once finished eating, it transforms and vanishes; when the time comes, it reappears.
It flows on incessantly and continuously, coming and going without end. Having eaten, they proceed, first to harmonize the body so that it remains free from [sickness].
It is to settle and concentrate the mind, ensuring it does not become negligent, so that one may find leisure and attain its own true purpose.
When people of the world have finished eating, they either rush about with worldly affairs or increase their sleep; yet in that land, they practice walking meditation after meals.
One can thus imagine the spirit of liberation and the state of carefree ease found there. Someone asked: "If you say they are Bodhisattvas," and so forth.
This is the purity of love. Why, then, does it not mention clothing? The answer is: for those who are born through transformation within the lotus, their mindfulness accompanies them as well;
they do not require cutting, sewing, beating, dyeing, or washing, yet they possess immeasurable, most excellent garments.
Circlets, hairpins, and necklaces—various forms of adornment—and wondrous incense that fulfills all desires, universally perfuming sentient beings so that all are fully satisfied and satiated.

Without seeking clothing they obtain clothing; without seeking food they obtain food. Those sentient beings of this land who wish to enjoy the natural clothing and food of that country should reflect upon what is appropriate for them.
Thus, one must pray for the establishment of peace and stability in one's own person.
Regarding the station of life: first, bind your own mind with the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha" so that it does not stray for even a moment;
this is what constitutes a true disciple of the Buddha.
It is further said: "The offerings to the Buddha are called supramundane food. These are: first, the food of dhyāna-delight; second, the food of aspiration; third, the food of mindfulness;
fourth, the food of liberation; and fifth, the food of the joy of Dharma."
△ Third, the summary of the matters concerning the supreme bliss of Sukhāvatī. Śāriputra, the land of Sukhāvatī is adorned with such meritorious qualities.
This summary follows the preceding descriptions of celestial music, celestial flowers, and so forth; all these various adornments are due to Amitābha.
The Buddha’s true vows and the accomplishment of his deeds of practice are immeasurable.

If the sentient beings of this land were to collectively resolve their minds on the Way and proceed together to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, they would not let even a single meal or a single night pass in vain for the duration of their lives.
Therefore, in the past, the Layman Bai Xia Shan renounced his residence to establish a temple and donated his salary to transcribe and bestow one thousand copies of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
Whenever he prostrated before the Buddha, he would recite aloud: "In the Pure Land of the World of Ultimate Bliss, there are no evil realms nor manifold sufferings;
may those like my own self, aged and infirm, be reborn together with the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. One can thus know the nobility [of his aspiration].
If even those gentlemen still rely upon that land, how much more so should we? If we do not again exercise self-reflection and vigilance.
△ Now, the sound of the Dharma was first proclaimed.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, in that land there are always various wondrous birds of diverse colors: white cranes, woodpeckers, and so forth.
Sparrows, parrots, śāris, kalaviṅkas, and jīvañjīvakas— these various birds, throughout the six periods of day and night,
utter harmonious and elegant sounds. These sounds eloquently expound such dharmas as the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment,
and the eightfold noble path.

The former statement regarding the various heavens presenting auspicious omens refers to the excellence of making offerings; this statement regarding birds and trees producing sounds refers to the excellence of hearing the Dharma.
"Various" means not being of a single kind. "Wondrous and marvelous" means that what emerges is extraordinary.
"Birds of variegated colors" refers to white cranes, peacocks, and the like. "Co-ming" (saṃjīva) is also called "life-and-life" (jīvājīvaka). Furthermore...
They are called "Cloud-born. As for these various birds, they cannot be fully enumerated even if one were to attempt to count them.
Day and night, these birds constantly produce elegant sounds, ceaselessly expounding and elucidating the subtle and wondrous meaning of the Dharma.

Apart from the sublime voice of the Buddha, among both devas and humans, no sound is beyond their reach; they understand all phenomena without exception. They are not like the birds of the human world.
Furthermore, although this land has parrots and mynas that can mimic human speech, these are merely birds that learn to talk;
they may speak, yet they do not understand the meaning, and thus they remain but flying birds. If even the Way of Humans is not yet mastered by them, how much less so the Buddha-dharma?
The birds of that country, however, are able to expound upon the five faculties and five powers of all Buddhas, as well as the seven factors of enlightenment.
This is the source of the Dharma of the Eightfold Noble Path.

As for the five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*): first is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*). With firm and steadfast faith, one realizes entry into the *dharmadhātu*, whereby karmic retribution is eliminated.
Second is the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*). Without retreating and advancing ever forward, one remains focused on this very point, single-mindedly upholding wholesome dharmas. Third...

The first is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*). Right mindfulness is firm and stable; coming and going without turning back, it is maintained with diligence and never abandoned. The fourth is the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).

Cultivating the mind without distraction, right concentration is unwavering, illuminating and shattering all states of existence (*bhava*). The fifth is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). Tranquil illumination is profound and still;
both person and phenomena are simultaneously forgotten, as one clearly discerns the biased and the correct.
The five powers are: first, the power of diligence, which neither devas nor humans can obstruct; second, the power of faith, which the paths of Māra cannot lead astray;
third, the power of mindfulness, which afflictions cannot touch; fourth, the power of concentration, which externalists cannot disturb;
and fifth, the power of wisdom, in which not a single thought-moment can arise [of delusion].
The seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are as follows: First is the enlightenment factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
When contemplating all phenomena, one is well able to discern the true from the false. Second is the enlightenment factor of vigor (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

When practicing great vows, one is well able to discern and does not erroneously engage in fruitless asceticism. Third is the enlightenment factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). When the mind attains the True Dharma, one is well...
1. It is the awakening that does not follow after the agitation of perversions. 2. It is the awakening of elimination;
when eliminating the afflictions of form-characteristics until they are exhausted, one is well able to awaken and does not lose the roots of goodness of right knowledge and right view.
3. It is the awakening of relinquishment; when having already relinquished the objects of entry, one is well able to awaken and never again recollect them. 4. It is the awakening of concentration.
Bodhi: when attaining meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one is well able to awaken to and comprehend stillness and clarity. Seventh is mindfulness of bodhi:
when practicing supramundane dharmas, one is well able to awaken to and penetrate deeply into concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*).

The Eightfold Noble Path consists of: first, the noble path of right view. This refers to the true awakening attained during the waking state, wherein one establishes the principles of the truths through wisdom, free from error or delusion. Second, the noble path of right intention.

This refers to the time when, having already seen the truth, one employs the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) so as not to obscure it, thereby attaining entry into *nirvāṇa*. Third, the noble path of right speech...
The Path: With a mind free from evil thoughts, one uses untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) to illuminate and shatter the three karmas of body, speech, and mind.
Fourth is the Noble Path of Right Action: with untainted wisdom, one completely eliminates all entanglements and abides in pure physical karma.
Fifth is the Noble Path of Right Livelihood: with untainted wisdom, one thoroughly removes the ten unwholesome paths and wrong livelihoods.
Sixth is the noble path of right diligence: through untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), one diligently practices vigor to hasten toward the realization of great enlightenment.
Seventh is the noble path of right mindfulness: through untainted wisdom, one clearly understands the perfect awakening that is neither characterized by marks nor devoid of marks.
Eighth is the noble path of right concentration: through untainted wisdom, one abides in and maintains perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
If one traces back each of these from the preceding, they all manifest according to the capacities cultivated by sentient beings on their respective stages;

thus, whether realizing the Great or the Small, each attains what is appropriate for them. Such dharmas include not only the twenty-five types of dharma-gates for realizing the Way previously mentioned, but further comprise the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, and the four bases of power, which together constitute the three [trainings].
The seventeen chapters are equal to all other dharmas. As for the four foundations of mindfulness:

the first is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body. One contemplates that the nine orifices of the body constantly flow with impurity, and takes the realization of the Buddha-nature as the standard.
The second is called the foundation of mindfulness of sensation. To be addicted to and attached to physical forms is the cause of suffering; one must always [be mindful of this].

Taking purity as the standard. Third is the application of mindfulness to the mind: observing the arising and ceasing of the mind; taking it as the standard that the mind follows objects but does not fall into delusion or confusion.
Fourth is the application of mindfulness to phenomena: awakening to the equality of these phenomena, up to the realization that their self-nature is non-dual;
taking this as the standard.

The Four Right Efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*) are as follows: first, the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*), which is the resolve never again to give rise to evil thoughts that have arisen throughout one’s life;

second, the awakening of diligence (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), which is to eliminate ignorance at every moment so that it is not yet destroyed; third, the power of diligence (*vīryabala*), which is to cause wholesome states of mind that have not yet arisen to arise and become fully perfected;
fourth, right diligence (*samyag-vīrya*), which is to pray for sudden enlightenment so that wisdom that has not yet manifested may quickly appear.
The four bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) are as follows: first, the concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi*), which is the aspiration to attain the Buddha-way;

second, the concentration of effort (*vīrya-samādhi*), which is the dedicated cultivation for the sake of attaining the Buddha-way; third, the concentration of mind (*citta-samādhi*), which is the stabilization of the mind for the sake of attaining the Buddha-way.
The fourth is the Samādhi of Contemplation, through which one attains liberation and the Buddha-way.

This emerges from the Samādhi of the Compassionate Mind of all Bodhisattvas, serving to guide and receive sentient beings. It is the source of all thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that assist the path, benefiting both things and persons.
In that land, all the birds skillfully maintain the holy mind and eloquently expound the wondrous Dharma; thus one may know that land.

Not only did the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, and the great assembly of devas collectively teach through the three vehicles, but at times the various birds also simultaneously emitted the sounds of the Dharma, vowing that all sentient beings might together ascend to the other shore. Furthermore, these birds responded to conditions according to their karmic resonance.
For example, during the Sui dynasty, the monk Zhishun entered Mount Lu to cultivate the practice of purity; later, he lectured on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.

After completing his study of the *Six Contemplations Sutra*, he manifested illness. He saw parrots and peacocks circling his seat while reciting the names of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, emitting sublime sounds.
Knowing that the Way was accomplished, the Master told his disciples, "I shall attain rebirth in the Pure Land this very day. He then passed away while seated.
This is truly the Western Land where compassionate clouds are densely arrayed to receive and guide sentient beings; such is the state of those in the present world.

They, too, shall be moved to arouse the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), recollecting the Buddha and mindfulness of the Buddha, just as a mother remembers her child or a child remembers its mother;
may each fulfill their aspirations. For example, during the Tang dynasty, there was a nun named Jingzhen (淨真) from Hangzhou.
She resided at Jixian Temple in Chang’an and maintained the precepts and practiced mindfulness of the Buddha for over twenty years. One day she said to her disciples: "In the fifth month..."
Inside [the room], she saw the Buddha ten times and twice saw a youth playing upon a precious lotus flower.
She said, "I have already attained birth in the highest grade," and having finished speaking, she passed away. Thereupon, auspicious light of five colors appeared and dispersed after seven days.
At the same time, there was a woman named Zhang Tao, a native of Xiushui County, who was the second wife of the lay practitioner Changshui Shouyue. Her husband—

The wife recited the Buddha’s name without interruption every day. One day, when the layman went out to pay his respects at Putuo Mountain, she said to her two sons, "In my daily practice, I have contemplated the two phrases, 'This mind creates the Buddha' and 'This mind is the Buddha. Only now do I truly understand them.
On the fourth day, I shall depart. When the appointed time arrived, she sat upright and passed away. The following day, the layman returned and completed the funeral rites.
Afterwards, five blue lotus flowers emerged from atop the coffin; this was heard by those both far and near, all of whom sighed with admiration.
It is evident that even a woman could set her will upon the Western Land and fulfill her aspiration—how much more so should we, who possess the six sense faculties in full?
If we do not resolve to practice mindfulness of the Buddha and seek rebirth in the Buddha-land, how can we ever escape the cycle of birth and death?
It is like a body falling into a pit of fire; one should not think of staying but must quickly leap out, rather than allowing oneself to be burned to death.
Is a human being not superior to a bird?
Furthermore, it is said that the ten unwholesome paths consist of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—these are the three evils of the body—and false speech.
Frivolous speech, double-tongued speech, and harsh speech are the four evils of the mouth. Covetousness, anger, and delusion are the three evils of the mind.
△ Through vows and practice, one attains benefit.
The sentient beings in that land, having heard this sound, all mindfully recollect the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Regarding "that land," it refers back to the preceding text; it means that when the sentient beings hear this sound, they all [attain] the wisdom of the Buddha.
As for what is called "mindfully recollecting the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha," it is because the inspiration and benefits thereof are inexhaustible.
If hearing the sound of the Dharma brings no benefit, it is no different from worldly sounds;
yet, by hearing the sound and recollecting the Triple Gem, one comes to understand the meaning of the Triple Gem. There are two meanings of the Triple Gem: first, the mundane Triple Gem;
second, the supramundane Triple Gem. What is called the mundane Triple Gem refers to [images] carved, cast, modeled, or painted.
The Buddha Jewel. The yellow scrolls with red covers are called the Dharma Jewel. Bhikṣus who uphold the precepts in harmony and without dispute are called the Saṅgha Jewel.
As for the supramundane Three Jewels: that which is by nature a numinous awakening that illuminates and comprehends all phenomena is called the Buddha Jewel.

That which consists of the inherent virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and can be grasped and maintained is called the Dharma Jewel. That in which nature and characteristics are non-dual and quiescent—[is the Saṅgha Jewel].
Illuminating without contradiction is what is called the Jewel of the Sangha. These three are also known as the Supreme Vehicle and the Three Jewels of Self-Nature.
By practicing in reliance upon them, one immediately transcends the triple world. Because they are honored and revered by the world, they are called "Jewels.
As it is recorded in the *Tongshu*: "That which is most supreme is the Way; that which is most noble is Virtue. How much more so the Three Jewels—the Way and Virtue are infinite.
"Venerable One, could it not be called a treasure? Thus, when worldly people enter the Dharma-gate, they value taking refuge in the Three Treasures of their own nature (svabhāva).

If one constantly contemplates the Amitābha of one's own nature while walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, then one stands shoulder-to-shoulder with the Buddhas and has the Śrāvakas as companions.
Until such proficiency is attained, do not claim, 'I am a practitioner of the Buddha-recitation method.'"
Why? Because I resent how your mind clings to signs and every word clings to emotion.

Although you chant the Buddha’s name with others, this is merely the Small Vehicle of the worldly Triple Gem. To practice the true念佛 (nien-fo) of the Mahāyāna, you must set your mind upon ice-cold stillness and chant in deep secrecy.
Because the mind becomes utterly cold, it naturally becomes subtle; because the mind becomes utterly subtle, the mind...
Then one enters the subtle. Having entered the subtle, one finally realizes that the supreme vehicle, the wondrous Dharma that transcends the world, is truly difficult to transmit.
△ This explains the absence of the evil realms.
Śāriputra, do not think that these birds are actually born as the result of karmic retribution for their sins. Why is this?
In that Buddha-land, there are no three evil realms. Śāriputra, in that Buddha-land, even the names of the evil realms do not exist, let alone their actual presence.
All these various birds are transformations produced by Amitābha Buddha, who desires to cause the sounds of the Dharma to flow forth.
This is explained as being created through transformation. One might fear that what people call the Pure Land also contains animals;
however, since that Buddha-land has no three evil realms, how could there be animals? Since there are none, as for those mentioned such as white cranes and peacocks—what are they?
As for their origin, they reside in that land; tracing back their source, one finds they were manifested by the Buddha. As stated in the *Sixteen Contemplations Sutra*:

"The King of Wish-Fulfilling Jewels surges forth with subtle and wondrous golden light, which transforms into the radiance of a hundred jewels to become various birds whose Dharma sounds flow forth and proclaim themselves throughout the four quarters. This is because the Buddha’s mind is vast and great."
Desiring that the sound of the Dharma be all-pervasive and that the Dharma never cease, it is known that it is not only the Buddha’s grace that constantly bestows transformation and instruction,
but that he has also caused all the birds to together proclaim the wondrous Dharma of non-arising, so that there is no place or time where it is not heard.
Not only do sentient beings hear it and forever give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, abiding on the stage of non-retrogression, but so too do the devas.
Having heard this, they all wept, lamenting that they were not like the birds who skillfully uphold the Buddha-dharma and deliver sentient beings.
These birds, they realized, were all transformations produced by the great supernormal powers of Amitābha Buddha;
they were not merely worldly birds or animals. Someone asked: "If those in the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animal realm hear the Buddha..."
They are all born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. One may ask: "How is it that in that land there are no three evil realms? The answer is:

when an evil person follows the good, they are immediately called a good person; as for those within the evil realms, if they reach that land, they are immediately called new Buddhas—how could they still be considered evil?
If one relies on the perspective of non-duality, the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion are themselves precept, concentration, and wisdom.
Both the good and evil realms are entirely illusory; it is better to forget both person and phenomena and enter directly into the Pure Land.
This was like the Dharma Master Tanjian of the Song dynasty, who spent his entire life reciting the Buddha’s name with the vow to behold Amitābha.
One day, while in meditative concentration, he was graced by the personal visit of Amitābha Buddha, who washed his face with water and said: "I cleanse your defilements and wash your mind."
He thought: "My body and speech are now entirely purified. He then received a single lotus flower. When the Master emerged from samādhi, he took leave of the temple monks.

Sitting once more, he maintained a state where not a single thought arose and all phenomena were stilled. At the fifth watch, the assembly all heard the sound of the Master reciting the Buddha’s name, fading away as it traveled westward.
Thus, one may know that the essential words of reciting the Buddha’s name are not [merely for the sake of]... (the text here is incomplete).
In possessing manifold capacities, the most precious thing is for the single mind not to arise.
△ The Wind-Trees Expound the Dharma.
Śāriputra, in that Buddha-land, when a gentle breeze stirs the various jeweled rows of trees and the jeweled nets, they produce—

Subtle and wondrous is this sound. It is like hundreds of thousands of kinds of music playing simultaneously; those who hear this sound naturally give rise to thoughts of mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Sangha.
What was previously called the "canopy of jewel-trees" is here called the "tree-net.

When stirred by the wind, it produces sounds that guide and transform sentient beings through transformations like the songs of birds, providing inexhaustible benefit. "Wind is subtle" refers to the excellence of the wind;
"sound is sublime" refers to the excellence of the sound. With these sublime and elegant sounds, they harmoniously proclaim the various elements of the faculties, powers, and the path to awakening.
This is the Chapter on the Path. As for what is called a "gentle breeze," it seems to exist and yet seems not to exist;
it is neither cold nor hot, light and subtle, pure and harmonious, beyond all analogy. Moreover, those rows of trees and various jeweled nets are all composed of myriad treasures;
when struck against one another by the gentle breeze, they naturally produce subtle and wondrous sounds, like hundreds of thousands of musical ensembles.

To have them arise simultaneously is the height of elegance. It is said that the exquisite beauty of the sounds of celestial palaces and divine music does not equal the beauty of the sounds from the jeweled nets and moving trees in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

These sounds sometimes manifest as musical tones and sometimes as the sounds of the Dharma; all are due to the Buddha’s spiritual power, for the Dharma issues forth from the sounds of the trees and nets.
This refers to the teaching of the Dharma by Amitābha at all times, even when he does not speak.

If the sounds of the trees were not the sound of the Dharma, how could they cause sentient beings to recollect the Triple Gem? Furthermore, once sentient beings hear these sounds, their bodies and minds become sweet and joyful, and their sensual desires naturally vanish;
thus, they may be called the true sound of the Dharma. From this, one knows that in that land, it is not only...

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas constantly engage in the work of transformation and deliverance. Furthermore, from the jeweled nets upon which the trees and birds rest, all manner of adornments produce harmonious and elegant sounds, expounding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the various meanings of the dharmas that assist the path. For all sentient beings, [these sounds provide instruction].
Upon hearing this wondrous sound, they were all completely liberated and subsequently became Buddhas. Someone asked: "Seeing forms and hearing sounds are both not the Way;
by what means did those sentient beings become Buddhas? The answer was: "They did not take objects as objects, nor were they non-objects, nor were they not non-objects.
Therefore, it is said of old: 'When the mind can transform objects, one is identical to Suchness.'"
Come! When the mind is turned by external objects, even a Buddha is but an ordinary person. Thus, there is a verse that says: "The nature of hearing is itself empty;
the resonance of bamboo and the sound of the wind are all Dharma-speech. The objects of sight can be purified; the radiance of water and the light of the moon are all Zen mechanisms.
If a person wishes to hear the elegant music of that land, they need only take up a single phrase of the Buddha’s name and recite it directly. One must, above all, keep this in one's heart.
Without clinging to even a hair’s breadth of right or wrong—this is the foremost class of those with the power to attain rebirth. △ Fourth, the conclusion:
the simultaneous illumination of the facts and the principle of Sukhāvatī.
Śāriputra, that buddha-field is adorned with such meritorious accomplishments.
These various adornments—the harmonious sounds of birds and trees—are all the result of the merit achieved through Amitābha’s vows and practices during his causal stage.
Through this sublime assembly, he receives and guides the sentient beings of the great earth, leading them together to ascend to Sukhāvatī.
Whether they be men or women, those who possess the faculties for the Mahāyāna have long ago ascended to that land together,
without even needing to snap their fingers. Among them, those of inferior faculties cannot avoid the Buddhas bestowing compassion upon them once more,
manifesting their forms to guide them.
△ Questioning the Name and Revealing the Virtue:
Śāriputra, what do you think? For what reason is that Buddha named Amitābha? Śāriputra, the light of that Buddha is immeasurable;
it illuminates the lands of the ten directions without any obstruction. For this reason, he is named Amitābha.
What was stated above concerns the excellence of the *sāmbhogika-kṣetra* (the environment of retribution), upon which the great assembly relies to give rise to the correct [realization].

Now, regarding that land, Amitābha is its sovereign. The purport of this entire sutra is to enlighten worldly beings through the *nirmāṇa-prabhāsvara-samādhi* (the tranquil light samādhi) of Amitābha Buddha, thereby revealing his holy name and magnificent title of myriad virtues. Since its meaning is profound and vast, it ought to be proclaimed and disseminated.

Manifesting Virtue: At that time, the Buddha emitted from his body the light of virtue, the light of precepts, the light of meditative concentration, the light of the *uṣṇīṣa*, the light of wisdom, the light of samādhi, the light of guidance, and all manner of infinite and inexhaustible lights.
These universally illuminated the infinite worlds of the ten directions, all lands, and at all times; there were no sentient beings who, mindful of the Buddha, did not attain clear understanding.

It surpasses the sun and moon by hundreds of thousands of millions of times in its radiance alone. Reaching even into the realm of darkness, it is transparent and penetrating from within and without, such that nothing can obstruct it.
This is Amitābha Buddha, whose merit and wisdom are fully perfected, and whose phenomena and principle are perfectly integrated.
Like the vast moon in the water, he is serene, luminous, and pure. Contemplate this again and again; contemplate until there is no more to contemplate.
When emotions are severed and the mind is extinguished, what remains is a state of vibrant, lively aliveness; this is what is called "Buddha.
If one examines this principle, how can there be a distinction between that Buddha and this Buddha? How can there be the realm of persons? How can there be a Pure Land? How can there be Chan?
If people today can break through this barrier, they will immediately receive it intimately and realize it personally: Amitābha is...
Self-nature. Self-nature is Amitābha. An ancient said: "Morning after morning we rise together; night after night we embrace the Buddha and sleep.
If you have not reached this state, you will not only lose the enjoyment of the Pure Land, but you must fear losing your very life-root (*jīvamūla*).
Even through a thousand births and ten thousand kalpas, it will be difficult to recognize it again. If people today fear this...
I urge you most earnestly to make offerings to the Triple Gem, to receive and uphold the five precepts, and to cultivate the ten wholesome paths of action in unison.
Grasp and maintain the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha," whether reciting it silently or aloud, with one sound following the next, and with every thought linked to the next.
Just as a hen brooding her eggs constantly maintains the warmth so that it does not cease, so too shall the practitioner naturally arrive in that land.
Their lifespan there shall be immeasurable.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the lifespan of that Buddha, as well as that of his people, lasts for immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
therefore, he is named Amitābha.
The preceding statement that "the light is immeasurable" is one sense of the term "immeasurable. Now, it is further indicated that the lifespan is likewise immeasurable.
However, as for the Buddha’s immeasurable lifespan, it is manifested by the Buddha according to the capacities of sentient beings; therefore, it cannot be fixed to any specific number.
Within this indefinite number, I shall provisionally cite one or two examples. Regarding the three types of lifespan: first is the "corresponding lifespan" (*ying shòu*);

second is the "retributive lifespan" (*bào shòu*); and third is the "Dharma lifespan" (*fǎ shòu*). What is called the corresponding lifespan indicates being subject to birth and death, having both a beginning and an end.
The retributive lifespan is obtained once and obtained forever; it has a beginning but no end. The Dharma lifespan is neither lifespan nor...
He is not subject to the span of life; he is without beginning and without end. Therefore, he is called Amitābha Buddha.
This is an ancient Buddha who has manifested his body and preached the Dharma for immeasurable kalpas, beyond all calculation, and remains present before us even now.
If one were to think that the Buddha’s lifespan could be limited, then neither devas nor humans would be able to fathom its measure; this is what is meant by "having a limit."
...its immeasurability. How much more so is the Buddha’s lifespan, which is exceedingly long and remote, not confined to ordinary numbers;
it may be called the "immeasurable of the immeasurable. As for the phrase "and his people," this is a skillful use of inverted syntax.
The Buddha is the Dharma King; rather than speaking of the great assembly, he speaks of "the people. This does not mean that the Buddha's lifespan is immeasurable, and furthermore—
The lifespan of the people is likewise immeasurable; therefore, it is described collectively by means of *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
An *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* is that which is beyond number. To speak in terms of countless multiples is simply to say it is immeasurable and boundless.
That Buddha’s self-nature is eternally luminous and his self-nature is eternally quiescent; spanning from antiquity to the present, quiescence and luminosity are non-dual.
One should say that his lifespan is the immeasurable of the immeasurable; is this not Amitābha Buddha?

Although he is an ancient Buddha from immeasurable kalpas ago, currently residing beyond ten trillion buddha-lands, he is in fact seated cross-legged within the minds of sentient beings in this Sahā world, solemnly unmoving, with true permanence manifest alone.
Why is it that people do not recognize one another when they meet face-to-face? Alas! The mind is originally the Buddha, yet we obscure our own minds;

the Buddha is originally the mind, yet we delude ourselves regarding our own Buddha. If people today say they have no aspiration [for enlightenment], they are fundamentally misunderstanding what is right before their faces.
Even if one simply recites the name of Amitābha ten thousand times day and night, naturally, within a single kṣaṇa, one will certainly behold the Buddha.
△ The attainment of the Way occurred many kalpas ago.
Śāriputra, it has been ten kalpas since Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood.
The preceding words have already fully explained the meaning of that Buddha’s superior virtues; however, it remains to be examined how much time has passed since that Buddha attained the Way.
As for the passage in the Sūtra stating "ten kalpas," this refers to a number that is immeasurable and boundless;

it is simply expressed as "ten kalpas" rather than being explicitly called "immeasurable and boundless. What the World-Honored One referred to as "ten kalpas from now" was merely a teaching given in response to the capacities and conditions of those present at that time;
it was certainly not a statement regarding an ultimate, definitive number. How much less so in that case...
The Buddha has attained enlightenment for an incalculable number of eons now. For example, the bhikṣu Dharmākara, who practiced and attained enlightenment, is none other than Amitābha Buddha.
Furthermore, the Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra states: "There was a wheel-turning king named Aśoka-manas (No-Contention-Thought)."
He made offerings to the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha. At that time, the king practiced the Way and received a prophecy from the Buddha, who said:

"After an eon as vast as the sands of the Ganges, you shall become a Buddha in a world in the western direction; your land shall be named Sukhāvatī. This king is none other than the present Amitābha Buddha.
Furthermore, the Mahāyāna Vaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra states: "There was a bhikṣu named Śuddhajīva..."
He who made offerings to that Buddha upon his attainment of enlightenment is none other than the present Amitābha Buddha. Furthermore, the *Bhadrapāla-kalpika-sūtra* states:
"At the time of the Tathāgata Meghasvara-nirghoṣa, there was a prince named Viśuddhapuṇyavipākasvararāja who made offerings to that Buddha upon his attainment of enlightenment;
he is none other than the present Amitābha Buddha. Moreover, the *Anantamudrā-dharmaparyāya-sūtra* says: "The Lion..."
When you were playing as the Tathāgata Golden Light, there was a king named Victorious Power (Jayaśrī) who made offerings to that Buddha upon his attainment of enlightenment;

he is none other than the present Amitābha Buddha. Furthermore, the Lotus Sūtra states that during the time of the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, there were sixteen princes who left the household life to seek the Way and all attained Buddhahood. The ninth prince—

This is none other than Amitābha Buddha as he is now. One should know that instances of Amitābha responding thus to the capacities of sentient beings through various teachings are too numerous to be fully enumerated.
The aforementioned points all concern ancient Buddhas from immeasurable kalpas ago who manifested at a single time;
therefore, the discussion of "ten kalpas" is merely a conventional number. By no means should one cling rigidly to the literal figure of ten.
I shall discuss this. However, these words are difficult for people of the world to believe. If you have doubts, let them rest for now.
What is the use of laboriously investigating whether the Buddha’s attainment was distant or near? It is essential only to investigate and clarify one's own nature (*svabhāva*).
Ultimately, why is it called "one's own nature"? Why is it said that one's own nature is the Buddha? If [one's own nature]...
The nature of one's own great matter of birth and death has not yet been clarified; this is ten thousand times more urgent than debating whether the Buddha is distant or near.
However, people today all apply their minds in error, constantly wandering through the cycle of worldly dust. Although they possess the same essence, it remains unclarified;
therefore, one should first attend to what is most urgent. For example, during the Song dynasty, there was a man named Fan Yan from Renhe County in Hangzhou.

Not only did he sever his mind from worldly affairs, but he even forgot his family business. Thinking only that he was a sojourner in this world, he cherished every moment of time and focused his mind exclusively on the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
One day, he suddenly beheld Samantabhadra Bodhisattva descending, riding upon a six-tusked white elephant.
The Bodhisattva immediately emitted a golden light from between his eyebrows and informed Huayan: "At the hour of the rabbit (dawn) tomorrow, you shall go to that place."
At the riverbank, after one night had passed, he saw the Buddha coming to welcome him; he then sat in meditation and passed away.

One must know that the ancients perceived the true nature of the path with such clarity that this day came to them. Why should people today not be like them? Recite the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion.
△ A general indication of his retinue:
Furthermore, Śāriputra, that Buddha has immeasurable and boundless śrāvaka disciples, all of whom are arhats;
they cannot be known by means of calculation. The multitude of bodhisattvas is likewise so.
The preceding passage repeatedly mentions the Holy Sovereign of the Land of Ultimate Bliss; this has already been clearly discerned.
However, a sovereign must have companions, and these companions are none other than the śrāvaka disciples. They are all noble sages among the four fruits of sanctity, and are thus called arhats.
As for the four fruits: the first is called the fruit of srotāpanna. Having entered the stream of birth and death, they cultivate the fruit of outflowlessness (anāsrava). Not...
Falling into the four modes of birth yet entering the stream of the sages, this is the Śrāvaka of the first fruit (srotāpanna). Second is the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin:
coming from the heavens, dwelling among humans, being born among humans, and departing to the heavens;
though beholding various objects with the eyes, they have not yet exhausted the cycle of arising and ceasing—this is the Śrāvaka of the second fruit. Third is the Anāgāmin...
The fruit of the *Sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returner). One is definitively no longer subject to rebirth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and has no further dharmas to learn;
this refers to the *śrāvaka* of the three realms. Fourth is the fruit of the *Arhat*. Both mind and objects are empty, and one does not undergo further existence;
this refers to the *śrāvaka* of the fourth fruit. "Further existence" (*punarbhava*) refers to future birth. The four fruits discussed above do not refer to [the specific individuals] pointed out.

The four individuals then spoke to explain the meaning of the four types of fruition stages. Furthermore, as for the Buddha’s retinue, even if one were to enumerate them, they could not be fully exhausted;
thus the Sūtra says, "They cannot be known by calculation," which is an extreme expression of their great number.

Therefore, all the sages are likened to the waters of the ocean, whose depth and source are difficult to measure. As for what are called the "multitudes of Bodhisattvas," these too are likewise [innumerable].

This can be calculated and known. Thus, the Sūtra says: "It is also like this. When many beings eventually attain Buddhahood, they emerge as those in their final birth before enlightenment (*ekajātipratibaddha*), as described in the following passage.
It should be understood that within the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the worthy and holy ones of the Three Vehicles all look up to a single Buddha;
the two truths, the ultimate and the conventional, both arise from a single mind. This single mind is perfectly clear, and merit is fully perfected.
Regarding the "Feet of Wisdom": when people today contemplate the state after closing their eyes [in death], they experience the suffering of being utterly bewildered and having no place to dwell.

Therefore, while still alive, one should naturally aspire to cultivate the practice of being a companion to the Bodhisattvas. If you wish to be born in that land, you must follow the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) and examine your own mind:
throughout a single day, how many thoughts follow the good, how many follow the evil, and how many thoughts are directed toward repaying the Three [Jewels]?
Precious Heaven and Earth! How many thoughts do I dedicate to repaying the imperial grace and the virtue of the Buddha? How many thoughts do I dedicate to repaying my parents, teachers, and elders?
How many thoughts do I apply to subduing the demons of affliction and enmity? How many thoughts do I apply to practicing and studying the bodhisattva path?

How many thoughts do I apply to realizing impermanence, suffering, and emptiness? How many thoughts do I apply to enduring hardship for the sake of establishing the Buddha-dharma? How many thoughts do I vow to bring to fulfillment?

At that time, the Buddha extensively delivered the masses from their delusions. He would daily examine how many thoughts were held in the precepts and vows to pay homage to the Buddha, and how many thoughts were dedicated to lighting lamps, burning incense, and scattering flowers.
Through such inspection, he knew that those who followed these words were few, while those who turned their backs on them were many;
they all remained caught within the conditions of their own emotions, departing with a mixture of knowledge and understanding. Thus, there was once a monk...
While single-mindedly cultivating pure karma, one should also examine the mind for its favorable and adverse states, using black and white beans as markers.
Whenever a virtuous thought arises, take one white bean; whenever an evil thought arises, take one black bean.

From morning until evening, if the black beans taken are more numerous, one must record the count each night and inevitably weep with tears streaming down. Before even a year has passed, [the result will be evident].
He took only white beans and did not take the black ones. When this monk was approaching his death, a rare fragrance filled the room, and celestial music welcomed him as he ascended to the Pure Land.
Someone asked: "If one seeks birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, why must one necessarily possess such a virtuous mind?
He replied: "Mencius said: 'To wear the robes of Yao, recite the words of Yao, and practice the deeds of Yao—'"
It is simply Yao. To study the Way of the Buddha is to follow the conduct of the Buddha; thus, the mind itself is the Buddha.
△ Summary of the ultimate principle and meaning of Sukhāvatī:
"Śāriputra, that Buddha-land is adorned with the accomplishment of such meritorious virtues."
As stated above, regarding the manifestation of virtue through light, the śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas exert themselves in various forms of adornment;
these are all accomplished through the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of Amitābha Buddha’s vows and practices.

Just like the radiant splendor of the sun and moon, they pervade heaven and earth, illuminating and shattering all the delusions and darkness of sentient beings, thereby causing every person to give rise to [the aspiration for enlightenment].
The Bodhicitta. In the future, one will certainly attain ultimate Buddhahood.
△ Awakening the great assembly:
Furthermore, Śāriputra, all those born in the land of Sukhāvatī are non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*).
Furthermore, following the preceding text, it says that the sentient beings in that land have all already been born there.

These "born ones" refers to those who have long cultivated the supreme multitude within the land, each attaining entry into the stage of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-ksanti*) and eternally realizing *avaivartika* (non-retrogression).
*Avaivartika* is precisely what is called the Ground of Non-Retrogression; it is the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom, which possesses the moisture of compassion and is able to—
It is complete; there is progress and no regression. All śrāvakas and bodhisattvas alike are born from the ocean of pure wisdom.
Regarding the assembly of humans, devas, and the immovable: "immovable" means non-retrogressive. However, within the stage of non-retrogression, there are distinctions of superior and inferior.
The superior is that which is eternally abiding by its own nature, non-dual with the Buddha, and possesses a lifespan of eternal kalpas. This is indeed—

"Retreat is non-retreat. There are three meanings of "inferiority": first, if one has destroyed the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), one will never again lose the status of a transcendent being;
this constitutes the stage of non-retrogression in status. Second, having subdued and severed the *rajas* (dust-like) afflictions, one will never again lose the practice of a bodhisattva;
this constitutes the stage of non-retrogression in practice. Third, when ignorance (*avidyā*) has been destroyed...
They never lose the right mindfulness of the Middle Way; this constitutes the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). They possess only progress and no regression;

therefore, it is said that they are all *avaivartika*. These members of the superior assembly all fully possess the thirty-two marks, their faculties are clear and sharp, and they proceed directly to the attainment of Buddhahood without ever falling into the evil realms. This is not due to the power of recollecting the Buddha alone.
It cannot be otherwise. If people of today can maintain the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation), they shall attain birth in that land and abide in the stage of non-retrogression.

By relying on this sublime and swift shortcut to transcendence, one suddenly departs from the state of suffering-abounding and joy-scarce, and of arising-and-ceasing impermanence—is this not indeed a source of great joy? Therefore, regarding rebirth through *nien-fo*, people—
Regarding human affairs, if the sentient beings of this very Sahā world can truly, moment by moment, mindfully recite the Buddha’s name and,

moment by moment, contemplate the West, such that even at the time of death when they are oppressed by suffering and pain, their only thought remains focused on reciting the Buddha’s name with the intent to go to Sukhāvatī,
they will truly be the foremost among those who have attained the stage of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, regarding the thirty-two marks: first, upholding pure precepts; second, cultivating the practice of giving;
third, not deceiving sentient beings; fourth, protecting the True Dharma; fifth, not disrupting the assemblies of others; sixth, offering exquisite garments as gifts;

seventh, offering pure food and drink as gifts; eighth, delighting in hearing the Buddha-dharma; ninth, concealing and bearing the faults of others; tenth, cultivating wholesome dharmas; eleventh, skillfully transforming [others].
12. Protecting sentient beings from fear; 13. Seeing those in need and joyfully assisting them; 14. Constantly practicing the ten wholesome paths of action;
15. Constantly bestowing medicine upon the sick; 16. Adorning oneself with wholesome dharmas. The above are the causes; the following are the results: 1.
Giving rise to an impartial mind; 2. Being harmonious and free from strife; 3. Attaining precious treasures spontaneously; 4. [The third]... the three... (text fragment).
1. Purity of karma; 2. Overcoming the faults of the five protective factors; 3. Accomplishing meritorious virtues; 4. Constantly using gentle speech; 5.
Cultivating a mind of loving-kindness; 6. Seeking the Path with a sincere heart; 7. Praising the merits of others; 8.

Honoring parents, teachers, and elders; 9. Delighting in preaching the Dharma; 10. Giving bedding and seats; 11. Refraining from discussing worldly affairs; 12. Receiving [instruction from] teachers and friends.
The Teaching: Sixteen do not undergo rebirth through unwholesome karmic additions.

△ Regarding those who lead others to rebirth, among them there are many who are in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*); their number is so vast that it cannot be known by calculation.
It can only be described through immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) numbers.

Regarding those within it: as stated in the preceding text, not only are the sentient beings of that land who dwell on the stage of non-retrogression beyond limit, but even the *parinirmita-bodhisattvas* (bodhisattvas in their final birth) therein cannot be known by means of calculation.
The assembly is even more vast than that of those who already dwell on the stage of non-retrogression; it is beyond comparison.
It is said to be as vast as an *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa. Yet, this description is difficult for people to believe. Why? Because it was previously stated that the Western realm is supreme.
The various adornments—the nets of trees, lotus ponds, palaces, and flocks of birds made of many jewels—are beyond measure;
they may be called the very pinnacle of abundance. One might fear that even that land would be unable to accommodate so many beings.
In response, it is said: "It is just as if someone were asked how many people there are in the Sahā world, and one were to reply: [and then remain silent].

Furthermore, this cannot be known through calculation; yet all people in this land know that [the number of beings] is exceedingly great, and even so, the land is vast and the population sparse—how can there be any doubt about this?

When the Buddha speaks of one who is "in their last birth before Buddhahood" (*ekajātipratibaddha*), he does not mean a single lifetime of transmigration for sentient beings in the present world, but refers only to the final stage of the Bodhisattva path, after which they shall succeed to the rank of Buddha.

This refers to the stage [of a Bodhisattva]. Regarding those who will attain the fruit of the Way in one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*): they are like Śrāvakas at the third fruit who have not yet exhausted all births.

Only upon attaining the fruit of Arhatship does one sever future existence (*punarbhava*). Although future existence is severed, one has not yet attained Buddhahood; therefore, it is called "one birth remaining until the place of succession" (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

This means entering the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*) to succeed to the rank of a Buddha. This is what is meant by "transferring to the position of a Buddha. The World-Honored One addressed the assembly above...
Within this [assembly], there is further mention of beings who are "in their final birth" (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

This indicates that they possess an even deeper resolve, being encouraged and hoping to enter together into the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) while awaiting their succession to the position of a fully enlightened Buddha (*buddhapada*). Someone may ask:
"If that is so, then how is it that Maitreya Bodhisattva will succeed to the supreme position in the future, while Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva will succeed to that [position] in the future?"
It is a land. As for the Bodhisattva Shi (Śāntamati), he will succeed him next. It is not yet known where sentient beings who attain Buddhahood will succeed [the Buddha].
The answer is: those who succeed are not necessarily restricted to the realm of Amitābha; the worlds of the ten directions are inexhaustible.
The nirvana of all Buddhas is inexhaustible, and the Bodhisattvas who occupy the position of succession are likewise inexhaustible.

To dwell within that land awaiting such a position—how could this not be called possible? If a person of today were to make a firm vow to become a Buddha, they need only seek a clear understanding through the single phrase of the sacred name "Amitābha Buddha," thereby suddenly realizing that one's own nature is oneself as Buddha. This too is so.

This is one who is in his final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*). It is sufficient to see that the Buddha’s grace and protective mindfulness toward sentient beings ensure that not a single person is lost;
this may be called the ultimate pinnacle of transcendent excellence. Someone asked: "Sentient beings and the Buddha are both insentient (without emotion);
for what reason does the Buddha love sentient beings to such an extent? The answer was: "It is not only the Buddha's mind that is thus. As it is said:
Confucius said: "One cannot associate with birds and beasts; if I am not among these people, with whom shall I associate?

This is precisely the heart of the Buddha. One can thus know that the ancient sages and former worthies bestowed their profound grace and instruction, wishing for all people to leave the sea of suffering early and thereby fill the seat of Buddhahood.
People must keep the sages' grace in mind and swiftly take up a single phrase of the Buddha's name.
Contemplate day and night; at every moment of thought, ask, "Who is this? Contemplate thus, examine thus.

When, in a single morning, the bottom of the bucket falls out, you will truly enter the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). Once having entered, your mind shall become even more diligent to ensure that you never again fall back;
only then will you be one who perpetuates and flourishes the lineage of the Buddhas.
△ Furthermore, he exhorts them to resolve upon and practice with vigor.
Śāriputra, those sentient beings who hear this should make a vow, vowing to be born in that land.
While the preceding passage showed the correct Dharma to be practiced through principle, the present statement exhorts further the vigorous practice of the correct Dharma.
When sentient beings hear this sutra, they should truly give rise to great vows, vowing to be born in that land.

This constitutes the first level of exhortation. As for what is meant by "exhortation," it is stated repeatedly within this very sutra: there is the exhortation to hear and the exhortation to believe.
The exhortation to aspire and the exhortation to practice are most ultimate. Now, furthermore, there is the exhortation to generate the aspiration.

Because sentient beings act without sincerity and because their aspirations are not genuine, the Buddha has uttered these words. Herein, I shall briefly set forth four principles for generating and initiating the aspiration.
First, those who now first hear this sutra should rely upon the cultivation of the supreme excellence of Sukhāvatī.
First, those who hear this sutra make their vow based on the teaching that [the Buddha] brings benefit.
Second, those who hear this sutra make their vow based on the teaching that by single-mindedly holding the Name, rebirth [in the Pure Land] is certain.

Third, those who hear this sutra make their vow based on the teaching that by hearing and holding the Name, they are protected by the Buddha and shall not regress from Bodhi. Fourth, those who hear this sutra...
This refers to generating a vow based on the conviction that the teachings regarding the certainty of fulfilling one's aspirations are even more real.

One should understand that when the Buddha preached this sutra, every word was repeated and every phrase offered a renewed exhortation; with each hearing it became deeper, and with each vow it became more earnest.
His compassion for sentient beings was profound and his instruction of others tireless. These three—faith, vow, and practice—are the very provisions for the Pure Land.
One must ensure that everything is fully provided for without deficiency; only through true faith, true vows, and true practice can one achieve inconceivable merit.
Therefore, Amitābha Buddha’s vast salvation of sentient beings is also due to his Forty-eight Vows.
Even Samantabhadra Bodhisattva has a vow which says: "When I am about to reach the end of my life, may I completely eliminate all..."
Even if there are obstacles, one will see that Buddha Amitābha face-to-face and immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
Furthermore, one will see Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, and others; each of them has specific vows and verses regarding rebirth in the Pure Land.
The causes and effects of the three realms all revolve according to one's vows. Thus, as one’s vow may be, one receives celestial bliss; the impoverished mother was reborn in heaven.
Aspiring to become a Lord of the Underworld, the spirit of Mount Tai came to govern the ghosts. For those who study, their names are inscribed upon the Golden Tablet;

for those devoted to agriculture, they find joy and profit in their fields and gardens. If sentient beings wish to go to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, they need only rely on faith, vows, and diligent practice to arrive there.

It can be known that during the Song dynasty, there was the Venerable Master Ciyun, a repentance master from Lin’an County. His learning and conduct were noble and ancient, his fame surpassing that of all in the two provinces of Zhejiang.

He was single-mindedly devoted to the Pure Land and frequently practiced the *pratyutpanna-samādhi*, remaining for ninety days without sitting or lying down, focusing his mind solely on the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
Due to the exhaustion of his spirit, he contracted a hemorrhagic disease. Later, when he entered the ritual hall, the skin of both his feet...

The wound split open. The Master made a further vow, setting death as his limit. Suddenly, while in meditative concentration, he saw Avalokiteśvara extending a hand, pointing toward his mouth and drawing out several worms.
The Bodhisattva then poured nectar-water into the Master’s mouth. Thereafter, his illness was healed.
His body and mind became doubly serene and tranquil. With single-minded focus on the non-dual, one day in his later years he saw the Buddha coming to welcome him to the Pure Land, and he passed away.
Furthermore, during the Song dynasty, there was a lay practitioner named Wu Zicai. After retiring from official service, he vowed to be reborn in the Pure Land.
He prepared a coffin in advance and slept within it at night, instructing a youth to strike the coffin every night at the fifth watch.
The song says: "Wu Zicai, go back and return! There is no peace in the three realms; they cannot be dwelt in. In the Western Pure Land there is the lotus womb.
Later, he passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name without illness. All who attain rebirth do so because their vows have been fulfilled.
If people today recite the Buddha’s name but cannot proceed directly to that land, it is because they still lack sufficient faith, vow, and practice; it is due to the shallowness of their faith.
One’s vows are meager while one’s actions are many and one’s progress is slight.

Should one’s vows fail to be firm and steadfast, one should reflect upon how, in this very life, one will experience all manner of illness and suffering, grow old and decrepit, stumble and falter, utter erroneous words and be rebuked by others, and give rise to a single evil thought.
One cannot avoid being tortured by King Yama. Once life ends and the faculties are destroyed, one's closest kin and flesh-and-blood relatives stand by with hands folded in helplessness;
all precious treasures and family estate become the property of others.

Recalling this, even while currently amidst the midst of extreme suffering, one’s power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) may remain firm. Therefore it is said: "Action arises from aspiration; aspiration arises from faith (*śraddhā*); faith..."

From wearying of suffering and yearning for joy, one possesses true faith. If a person single-mindedly cultivates pure karma and attains birth in that land, not only is the Buddha their most intimate parent, but they shall also forever be free from all suffering and affliction.
Although it is said that that land is a distance of ten trillion leagues away, provided one lacks nothing in the three—faith, vow, and practice—the Pure Land is [attained].
It is right before one’s eyes. Thus, the Sūtra says: "The Western Land is this very land; this land is the Western Land.
Yet these two lines contain a profound barrier; without a single instance of faith and practice, how could one pass through it?
Because this is a Dharma that is difficult to believe and difficult to practice, the Buddha offers exhortations and vows, urging people to recite the Buddha's name. This is what he exhorts.
Those who seek to go to that land are like travelers in a foreign land who ought to return to their native home.
If people truly desire to return together to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, they should all follow the established vows of the ancients; how could they not then have a share in that Buddha-land?
△ To explain the reason for this:
Why is that? It is because one has been able to assemble together in one place with such superior and virtuous people.
This statement follows the preceding text which exhorted people to make a vow to be born in that land, because within that land there are these [beings].
Because those of the highest virtue assemble in one place, once a person has been born in that land, they enter such a sublime assembly, which is difficult for people to encounter;
therefore, one should seek birth in that land as it is the portion allotted to them. Someone may ask:
"The Sahā world is also a Buddha-field; why must one go so far to be born in another land? The answer is: "As for the land..."
There are three meanings. First, there may be lands where humans, animals, ghosts, and those in the hells dwell together;
it is not necessarily the case that all inhabitants are human. Second, there may be lands inhabited exclusively by humans, yet it is not necessarily the case that all are virtuous.
Third: There may be lands inhabited solely by virtuous people, yet not all of them are of the highest virtue;
therefore, those now called "all the most excellent people" (śreṣṭha-satpuruṣa) are not merely the virtuous among men, but rather the most excellent among the virtuous.

To the places where the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas listed above, as well as all the supreme virtuous beings up to those in their final birth before buddhahood reside, people of the present day may also go;
there they shall gather together in one place, walking hand in hand with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra were personally his supreme friends; how much more so for us humans today, who even when choosing where to dwell select a neighborhood of virtue (*li ren*).

If one does not seek rebirth in the Buddha-land after death, why would one? If a person wishes to ascend to the same realm as all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they should swiftly make great vows and practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name (*nianfo*) with true application. To reach the Buddha-land in a single day is truly like being released from a cage.

The bird flies away; by taking the ordinary as the holy, one is like a farmer acting as a courtier—every movement of the eyes and every step taken is nothing other than being within the ranks of the noble.

This statement follows from the preceding text; it merely says that ordinary beings can easily achieve the fruit of the Path, but it does not say that all possess the ease [of attainment] through merit.
One fears only those with little merit: even if they have accumulated goodness, they may still find it difficult to draw near. Why?
How much more so for an assembly of the most supreme virtuous people! How could one participate with but little goodness or little merit?

If one considers the essentials of entering the Way to be the arousal of the bodhicitta and the diligent, persistent recitation of the Name—maintaining this in every thought without deviation as the primary practice—and the concurrent cultivation of myriad virtues and merits as auxiliary practices for the Pure Land, yet cultivates only those myriad virtues and merits...
Those who do not uphold the Name will certainly have no way to go to the Pure Land; that land cannot be reached except through wisdom.
Those who single-mindedly uphold the Name but lack the merit of the myriad virtues will certainly be unable to attain the ultimate fruit;

One will attain Buddhahood before long. However, to cultivate only the auxiliary practices while lacking the primary practice is the cause for the finite fruits of humans and devas;
