Although there is no attainment of the ultimate fruit, this is but a minor loss. Even with the affliction of such a minor loss, those in the stream of those who will attain Buddhahood in their next life may still hold hope.
Why is this? Long ago, during the time of the Buddha, there was an old man who came seeking ordination.
At that time, Śāriputra and the other great disciples all refused to grant him the tonsure, observing that he had many kalpas remaining.
Because he lacked roots of goodness, the Buddha himself delivered this old man, who immediately realized the fruit of the Way. The Buddha told his great disciples:
"In immeasurable kalpas past, this person was a woodcutter. When he encountered a fierce tiger that pressed upon him in extreme danger, he was terrified and climbed a tree;
there, he uttered the name of Amitābha Buddha once. This too was a root of goodness, owing to me."
Having attained deliverance, one can see that even a small good deed, such as a single recitation of the Buddha’s name, later yields great fortune amidst hardships.
This is precisely what is meant by the saying: "A single recitation of the Buddha's name can eliminate the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.
Thus, the Sūtra states: "To once call out 'Namo Buddha,' all shall together attain the Way of the Buddha"—this is no false word. Therefore, one should uphold...
This name serves as proof that one may perform much goodness and much merit.

Although even this small good deed of an elderly person is fortunate enough to be saved by the Buddha, those who recite the Buddha’s name today seeking rebirth in that land must not harbor expectations of such specific benefits;
for fear of disappointment, they should instead cultivate the power of auxiliary practices to achieve the excellence of inconceivable merit.

Practice. Just as a boat sailing with the current and with the sails unfurled can enter the Land of Lotus directly and join the supreme assembly, so too, in correct practice, there should be no deficiency in auxiliary practices.

Those who wish to maintain the merit of auxiliary practices should filially support their parents, serve their teachers and elders, refrain from killing with a compassionate heart, sincerely cultivate the ten wholesome actions, uphold the Three Refuges, and be fully endowed [with these virtues].
One should observe the precepts, resolve for Bodhicitta, have deep faith in cause and effect, recite and study the scriptures, diligently perform prostrations, and exhort others to practice.
For this reason, the World-Honored One specifically distinguishes these from other practices and earnestly exhorts the world to "practice all good deeds."
The very root of humanity is to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name; it is the ladder for transcending the world.
△ This is the direct instruction on the correct practice:

If for one day, or two days, or three days, or four days, or five days, or six days, or seven days,
you maintain single-mindedness without distraction.

The preceding passage spoke of how many virtues and much merit lead to rebirth in that land; yet, cultivating various roots of goodness and planting various seeds of merit are difficult to practice and difficult to perform.
Therefore, the single method of mindfulness of the Buddha is specifically shown—direct, simple, and easy, which nurtures the roots deeply.
It requires nothing more than holding the name with a single mind throughout the day; this alone constitutes great virtue and great merit, a most excellent achievement.
This is virtue. When the Sūtra speaks of "good men and good women," it refers collectively to all sentient beings.
Regarding those who hear the teaching of Amitābha Buddha and uphold his name, this is addressed with earnest exhortation; it is my deep aspiration for all sentient beings.
Each should resolve with a firm mind to seek birth in that land, never succumbing to indolence.
The period of one day up to seven days is established because the faculties of sentient beings in this land vary from sharp to dull and their minds are often deluded and distracted;
it is spoken of in consideration of those of inferior capacity. However, if there are individuals of the highest faculties who hear that their own nature is itself Amitābha...
According to the teaching of [Avalokiteśvara] Bodhisattva, in the mere blink of an eye one may thoroughly illuminate the realm of the Buddha and swiftly ascend to the other shore;
why, then, impose the limit of a single day? Those of middling and inferior capacities cannot avoid striving to achieve accomplishment, yet this intention is not misleadingly shown.

It is simply because capacities are sharp or dull that the lotuses are divided into nine grades: three superior, three middling, and three inferior. Thus are the nine grades of transformational birth.

As for what is called "seven days," it is because one prays that the karmic practices cultivated by these nine classes of sentient beings may all be fully perfected, so that they may be ranked equally with the Buddhas.
Someone might ask: "The cultivation of Bodhisattvas requires a firm resolve spanning many kalpas before they can achieve the Way.
For people of the present age, whose spiritual foundations are most shallow, why limit it to seven days? The answer is: Seven...
The "days" are called the "small assemblies," lasting for two weeks, three weeks, or even up to seven weeks.
These are called the "great assemblies," which include the period of the *pratyutpanna-samādhi* lasting ninety days; alternatively, they may be performed in successive layers.
Although it is said to be "seven days," there is no fixed number. This count of seven is what is commonly spoken of in the world, just as when the World-Honored One traveled throughout the world.
Seven steps. The sutra describes seven rows of trees; the mantra is recited seven times. Regarding these "sevens," to speak by way of analogy:

those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha according to this fixed limit specifically refer to the actual practice of single-mindedly holding the name. As for "single-mindedness," there are many varieties.
It means that while vocally reciting the Buddha’s name, one does not depart from it day or night, and the mind remains continuously linked with the name of the Buddha.

Dense and continuous, without any other mental engagement—this is the middle-of-the-middle grade. To practice mindfulness of the Buddha by visualizing the golden countenance, or to practice mindfulness of the Buddha upon seeing the Buddha, or to practice mindfulness of the Buddha when encountering danger, peril, or oppression—this is the lowest-of-the-low grade.
By inferring from this, the remaining seven grades may be understood. What is called the single method of mindfulness of the Buddha is direct, straightforward, simple, and easy.

This refers to the Supreme Vehicle (Mahāyāna) for understanding birth and transcending death. People say that practicing Chan (Zen) brings an end to birth and death, yet they do not realize that the Pure Land also brings an end to birth and death.
Therefore, do not turn your back on the Pure Land while practicing Chan; do not turn your back on Chan while seeking the Pure Land. As the ancients said:
"If one has Chan but no Pure Land, I fear nine out of ten will go astray. If one has both Chan and the Pure Land..."

Like a horned tiger, Chan requires the certification of a Buddha, and the Pure Land must be realized through Chan. Therefore, regarding the source of this sutra, the emphasis is placed on the recitation of the name.
As for the recitation of the name, the emphasis lies in being free from signs and transcending all attachments, such that the mind is undisturbed and unified.
If there are those who are unable to maintain a single-minded focus, they may recite the Buddha’s name while their minds are distracted; yet even with a distracted mind, one cannot help but recite.
With every thought, one becomes pure and true; with every thought, one attains liberation. Therefore, the World-Honored One has provided a solemn exhortation for sentient beings in advance:
first to give rise to the three—faith, aspiration, and practice—as an aid to achieving an unwavering single-mindedness. Thus it is accomplished.
This is the foundation of the Way. Someone asked: "All Buddhas save sentient beings; why then do we recite the name of only one Buddha? The answer was:
"Humans harbor notions of 'self' and 'other,' but the Buddha-mind is without self. If one recites the name of one Buddha, all Buddhas will know it.
It is like a room where hundreds of thousands of bright mirrors hang high on all four walls, and a single lamp is lit in the center."
Each mirror reflects a single lamp facing it; thus, it is said that by recollecting one Buddha, all Buddhas are correspondingly recollected.
This is likewise the case here. However, those who necessarily recollect only this one Buddha do so because the minds of sentient beings in this land are easily confused and distracted.
Today they love this, and tomorrow they love that; how could they possibly maintain a single mind without distraction? For this reason...
Master Lianchi said: "If attachment is not profound, one will not be born in this Sahā world; if mindfulness is not singular, one will not be born in the Pure Land.

As for 'single-mindedness,' it means binding the mind to mindfulness with every thought, so that all emotional attachments are emptied. When emotional attachments are emptied, there is nothing left to be mindful of."
One who is free from all conceptualization is such that the mind and the Buddha are non-dual; this is called "single-mindedness" (*ekacitta*). This is the highest of the high grades.
By means of this very single-minded recitation of the Buddha's name, all manifold conditions are naturally relinquished—this is the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).

By means of this single-minded recitation of the Buddha's name, all evils naturally cease—this is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). By means of this single-minded recitation of the Buddha's name, one's own mind becomes supple.
To single-mindedly recollect the Buddha is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), for one never again falls back.

To single-mindedly recollect the Buddha so that no other thoughts arise is the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*). To single-mindedly recollect the Buddha is the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
Clear and distinct right mindfulness is precisely the Prajñāpāramitā. Single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha is to be tranquil and unmoving.

Single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha is to be pure and signless. Single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha, with every thought being mindless, constitutes the perfection of all practices and the accomplishment of the Samādhi of the Single Seal. This Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha is perfectly round and complete.
Ah, how radiant and brilliant! The *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi) is true emptiness that is not empty, and wondrous existence that is not existent.
The *nien-fo samādhi* is that which brilliantly illuminates itself, standing alone and solitary.
The *nien-fo samādhi* is precisely what Emperor Wu of Liang asked the Patriarch Daowu: "Who is it that faces me? To which the Patriarch replied: "I do not know. This is the *nien-fo samādhi*.
This is what Confucius said: "I have a single thread that runs through all my teachings. Zengzi replied, "Yes.
The *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi) is precisely the World-Honored One holding up a flower and Kāśyapa smiling. The *nien-fo samādhi* is precisely what the Sixth Patriarch said:
"I have a thing; when called upon, it does not respond. It is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white; neither male nor female."
"Phenomena! All these various responses you have given are indeed a form of samādhi. Now I, a junior student, also have one sentence as a response.
I do not know whether you, Elder, will act as my witness? Let me say this. [He drew a circle. "The Perfect Circle! Once more, a shout! (咄)
"△The Buddha appears before me.
This refers to the person at the time of their death; Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy ones, will appear before them.
"That person" refers back to the individual mentioned in the preceding passage who is able to hold the Name. This is because the preceding text merely stated...
"With single-mindedness and without distraction. This refers to the time of death, when one is able to behold the Buddhas appearing before them to welcome and lead one to rebirth in the Pure Land.

Regarding the Buddha’s descent [into this world], there are several meanings. First, because of the individual themselves, who possesses the power of faith and aspiration and a profound mind for practice in their daily life, the Buddha does not contradict his own original vow. His vow states: "Sentient beings of the ten directions..."
Regarding those who have made the vow to be born in my land: at the time of their passing, I shall not attain perfect enlightenment until I appear before them, surrounded by a great assembly.
Second, as the sutra says: "I shall manifest in the form of a Buddha, a high official, or a bhikṣu."
O Youth, for those who attain liberation through their own bodies, the Buddha manifests his own body to preach the Dharma for them; this refers to either the True Buddha or an Emanation Buddha.

Bodhisattvas such as Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta may appear carrying golden platforms, silver platforms, banners, canopies, and celestial music, descending according to the needs of the occasion.
This occurs through the resonance between the power of the person who holds the Name and the power of the Buddha.

Because the Way interpenetrates all things, when an ordinary person’s life comes to an end, at the moment when the previous existence is about to pass away and the subsequent existence has not yet arisen, the realms of their past wholesome and unwholesome karma manifest before them;
this is an established principle. For example, for those who have committed the ten evil deeds or acts of rebellion, the hells manifest;

for those characterized by stinginess, greed, and jealousy, the realm of hungry ghosts manifests; and for those who observe the five precepts and practice the ten wholesome deeds, the human realm manifests.
The Buddha appears before one. If a person who recites the Buddha’s name truly maintains single-mindedness without distraction, then pure mindfulness will be perfected.
Within this very state of pure mind, how could one not see the Buddha coming to welcome them? Thus, the Sūtra says:
"If you remember the Buddha and recite his name, you will certainly see the Buddha both in the present and in the future. As for those whose mind and objects have both subsided, they are like...
When the water is clear, the moon comes of its own accord; when the mind is pure, the Buddha appears of his own accord. How can there be any doubt?

There is another treatise which states that those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha have, during their ordinary lives, minds that are not yet single-minded and have not yet shattered ignorance; thus, it is upon a deluded mind.
That which appears to be the Buddha coming is actually a mental demon; even those who are not true Buddhas may manifest such forms.
Such a person will certainly be unable to attain rebirth in the Pure Land. Therefore, those who practice nianfo must seek the guidance of an enlightened master;
the priority lies in discerning the correct path and one must not presume oneself to be right. If a person’s deluded mind is not yet exhausted and their afflictions are many, when they face death—
At the time of death, there are those who seek the Buddha but he does not appear; yet this is certainly not because the Buddha has violated his original vow.
The Buddha indeed comes, but people themselves fail to see him. Why is this? It is because they delude themselves regarding their own Buddha-nature. Thus, Master Lianchi said:
"From time to time he reveals himself to those of the age, yet the people of the age do not recognize him. Those who practice nien-fo today must surely keep in mind the moment of death.
To see the Buddha, you must personally rely on the Dharma and single-mindedly hold his name; only then will your vows be decisively fulfilled.

If you do not diligently cultivate your vows, you will not meet the Buddha when the end comes. Should you instead be invited by those with ox-heads and horse-faces, would that not be a source of great pain?
Nevertheless, in the past there was Zen Master Dun Yunfeng, who was seized three times by King Yama; the Master remained solely in meditative concentration, manifesting a golden...
The stupa did not comply with its summons; it ultimately departed for the Western Land itself. However, if one wishes to emulate its example, one may not necessarily possess such power.
If you lack such power, from this day forward, practice with courageous diligence and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name.
△ I shall go to where the Buddha dwells.
When this person’s life comes to an end, their mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Utmost Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.

Regarding "this person at the time of death": based on what was stated in the preceding text—that the person who single-mindedly holds the Name shall see the Buddha come to welcome them at the end of life and go directly to that land—the sutra reiterates these words and praises such a person most highly.
Because they have gained mastery through right mindfulness during their daily life, at the time of death they experience no confusion or obstruction; for this reason, the Buddha [says]:
Recalling that person, it was through the power of their diligent practice and attainment. As for what is called "inversion," how is it inverted?

It is like failing to cultivate right mindfulness during one's ordinary days, allowing random delusions to arise, and having a mind that is largely distracted. Throughout one’s life, one harbors evil thoughts;

thus, at the moment of death, an evil realm manifests before one. This is what is meant by being at the mercy of the ox-headed and horse-faced messengers, who drag one away and command one’s every move.

Consequently, their minds become bewildered and confused; those who ought to enter hell encounter mountains of knives and trees of swords, cauldrons of oil and rivers of blood, yet they perceive these as gardens, groves, flowers, and ponds.
Those who are destined for rebirth as animals see the bellies of horses and the wombs of donkeys, yet they regard them as palaces and towers.
Thus, when confronted by thousands of such afflictive environments, their hearts rejoice and they rush headlong toward them, undergoing this suffering.
Regarding karmic retribution: riding upon these inversions, one undergoes birth within the three realms and seven destinies according to one's karma, with no end in sight.

Now that you have been able to meet a senior practitioner who can maintain single-mindedness without distraction, your internal right mindfulness will become concentrated and you will externally receive the welcoming reception of the Buddha.

Upon casting off this reward-body (*vipākakāya*), one will be reborn in that land after passing through a single lifetime. One may trust the Buddha’s words: "As the mind is pure, so is the Buddha-land pure.
Thus, everything encountered by the eye is the Land of Ultimate Bliss; hence it is said that all lands are merely according to where one's aspirations lie.
If pure mindfulness is perfected, one will be born by transformation within a lotus flower. This is what is meant by the inconceivable merit of *buddhānusmṛti* (recollection of the Buddha).

This is certainly beyond doubt. Someone asked: "Throughout the past and present, practitioners have all maintained the recitation of a single Buddha-name, and we see the predecessors of old departing along the path to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, shrouded in a subtle radiance. The fifth is the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣ-kaṣāya*). By means of this life-faculty, they lose their original resolve and turn their backs on the world in an instant; they are not the same as those who are ultimate.

All mantras spoken by the Buddhas are called "mind-seals" (cittamudrā). They are the secret mental records of the Buddhas for the purpose of delivering and guiding sentient beings;
they are what people today call "passwords. Since ancient times, translators have recorded the sounds using Chinese characters without recording their meanings, and thus there are no commentaries.
When people of China recite and uphold these mantras, it is as if they were speaking directly to the Buddha.
Regarding local dialects: although one may no longer understand the meaning of the mantra, if the Buddha hears it, he perceives the speech of sentient beings clearly and distinctly.
His prostrations and entreaties are boundless; he immediately provides protection and refuge.

Therefore, when people recite the Mantra for Rebirth, Amitābha Buddha’s light covers the crowns of their heads, guarding them day and night so that enemies and obstructors find no opportunity to harm them.

Thus, for those who practice the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti), there is the deity Bai Ze who constantly protects their person; his light shines for forty li, and no malevolent spirits can approach them.
Therefore, those who recollect the Buddha attain constant peace and stability in this present life and, at the time of death, are spontaneously reborn in the Pure Land.
For this reason, the sutras and dharanis are linked together, perfectly integrating the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings so that no principle is left unprovided.
There is no benefit that does not reach all. It is our great fortune to have received the compassionate teachings bestowed by the World-Honored One in the past.
As for the single practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (*nien-fo*), it is not only those from ancient times among both monastics and laity who have upheld the Name and attained rebirth in that land;

such individuals are too numerous to mention exhaustively. Even within the present flourishing dynasty, there are those such as Dharma Master Bo-t’ing of Chih-yun Temple in Hang-chou, followed by Ju-shui and Ssu-ch’i.
Masters such as these, who devoted themselves exclusively to the cultivation of pure karma, all attained rebirth [in the Pure Land]; there are traditions available to verify this.
Among those whom I have personally witnessed is Vinaya Master Wenhai of Mount Hua in Nanjing. His conduct was lofty and pure, and his reputation was esteemed throughout the four quarters.
Throughout his life, he led the assembly in reciting the Buddha’s name day and night. When he reached the age of eighty, one day the assembly saw a wooden Buddha emitting light. The Master...
He took leave of the assembly, sat upright, and passed away. Furthermore, there was Master Juhong of Wensi Temple in Huai’an Prefecture, whose observance of the precepts was rigorous and strict.
He practiced *nianfo* (recitation of the Buddha’s name) and the release of living beings; whenever he encountered flying insects striking the water, he would invariably rescue them.

For forty years, day and night, the Buddha’s name never left his mouth, to the point that he neglected sleep. When he reached the age of over seventy, he knew in advance the time of his death and continued to recite the Buddha’s name.
He passed away while seated. Furthermore, the Master Hongchen of Puming Temple in Jiaxing constantly lectured on the inner scriptures throughout the ten directions.
He never grew weary of exhorting people to practice *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation). When the Master was in deep sleep, the sound of Buddha-recitation did not cease.

Whenever he saw his disciples, he would say, "I wish for you all to recite the Buddha's name for me at the time of my end," as an instruction to assist him in proceeding to the Western Pure Land. The Master was eminent...

In his later years, his spirit was serene. One day, he passed away from a slight illness; his eyes remained open as if he were still alive. When the disciples heard that their master had returned to the West, they did not assemble until evening.
Having finished discussing how to fulfill their master’s final wish, they chanted the Buddha’s name together for a short while, whereupon the master’s eyes closed of their own accord.
Furthermore, there was a man from Xiushui County named Lu Hongxun, who lived in Jiulihui Village. He made his living through the practice of medicine, yet he did not calculate for profit.
Whenever he encountered those who were poor or distressed, he would instead provide them with wealth to treat their ailments. By nature, he maintained a vegetarian diet and was filial and benevolent;

he diligently exhorted his entire family to observe the precept against killing and to release living beings. He recited the Diamond Sūtra daily and maintained a steadfast mind in the recitation of the Buddha’s name. When he reached the age of seventy...
For over ten years, one day he suffered a slight ailment. He bathed, changed his clothes, and commanded his successor to set up seats in the central hall.

He ordered his family members to stand in attendance on both sides—men to the left and women to the right—while he sat facing west reciting the Buddha’s name until he passed away. Among the predecessors mentioned above, how could such a thing have been possible unless they had practiced the pure karma of the Buddha’s name with sincere hearts?
Furthermore, I have heard that among monastics and laypeople near and far who recite the Buddha’s name, their deaths at the end of life were extraordinary and miraculous.
There are indeed many who have attained a fine reputation; however, as I have not yet verified these matters, I have not recorded them here. Recently, someone remarked:
"Why is it that some believe in *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) but do not believe in being reborn in that land?

It is because, having personally observed practitioners of *nien-fo*, I see that while they regularly perform virtuous deeds during their daily lives, at the time of their death, they remain quite ordinary. Alas!

Although he recites the Buddha’s name and speaks of virtuous matters, his goodness is still slight and meager. He does not understand that person’s mind, and there are many things he cannot speak of to others.
Moreover, since his recitation of the Buddha’s name is not yet single-minded, how can he be compared to the ancients?
If one were to recite the Buddha’s name with pure goodness and a single mind, such that the mind itself could no longer be apprehended—only then would it be comparable.

The awakened nature is neither existent nor non-existent; this is ascending to the Pure Land. Now, I (Liaogen) have meager merit and heavy obstacles, and my practice of reciting the Buddha’s name has been brief.
If the Buddha’s grace does not descend upon me, I pray only that I may go to the Land of Ultimate Bliss myself.
